The code is chosen on its own documented grounds rather than picked: it is "the code the contract reserves for shutdown, because the export's backend is the thing that went away", and 1011 "would report it as an unexpected relay failure" when the relay is healthy and the device is not. The cause is resolved **after** the peer-reset resolution, so a revocation still closes **1008** (M4-25) rather than being downgraded, and **before** the framing verdict, which outranks everything. **The scope is one caller, not the cancellation path.** An earlier cut of this fix defaulted on the *fact* of actor cancellation, which review showed reaches roughly twenty-eight distinct reasons — relay shutdown, authority outage, owner fence and device framing faults among them — and would have told a consumer "the device is not connected" while the relay was the thing that stopped. The remedy is a forward fix commit — never `--amend`, which would bury it. **It is the more dangerous mode on a branch like this one**, whose entire claim is guard redness: what was silently committed was a defeated guard rule, on a branch asserting that every guard rule is load-bearing. Every green run: the same session closed with **`CONTROL_CLOSED`**, `cause_present=true`, close **1012**. **Candidate (1) is excluded by measurement.** The Fin-or-Closed arm of that loop was taken in **0 of 24**; the pump left through `closed.cancelled()` in all 24. Control first: `disconnect_control` closes the session as `CONTROL_CLOSED` and the typed cause is published. **Data first:** the next frame bound for the device fails to queue, `protocol_failure` closes the session as `REVERSE_CHANNEL_UNAVAILABLE`, nothing is published, and the control disconnect that arrives afterwards is a no-op because the session is already gone. Same event, same consumer, two close codes. **The fix, and why it cannot re-broaden 1012.** The gate is **not** widened to the reason string. `queue_data` returns one failure for two unrelated events — the session's own queue **budget** refusing the bytes, which is the *relay* declining to buffer while the device is healthy, and the carrier's receiver being gone, which is the device's data socket having ended — and a string match would report the first as 1012 on exactly the opposite ground to the one `error.rs:273-278` justifies it by. That is the defect M4-28's narrowing removed, and re-creating it was this row's named hazard. So the publication is gated on the **fact** the string is ambiguous about: `reason == CONTROL_CLOSED` **or** (`reason == REVERSE_CHANNEL_UNAVAILABLE` **and** the carrier's sender reports itself closed, so the socket task that held its receiver is finished). A budget refusal leaves that sender open and still publishes nothing, and the roughly twenty-eight other reasons are untouched. The blast radius is one further reason in one sub-case. **What the discriminator guarantees, and in which direction it can err.** It reads the carrier's **current state at teardown**, not the trigger, and the three cases are stated rather than left to be inferred. A budget refusal while the device is up leaves the sender **observably open**, so nothing is published and the consumer keeps the close it had — that is the case the discrimination exists for, and it is guaranteed, not merely usual, because a refusal never touches the sender. A budget refusal followed closely by a **genuine** socket close does publish 1012, and that is **correct**: a closed sender means the task owning its receiver has finished, so the device's transport really is gone at the moment the consumer is told, and 1012 is true of the world then whichever failure tripped the teardown first. | M8-C07 | [x] Close the ACP export's process-group **trigger**; its **reach** stays open and is recorded as such. | implemented (verified local) | acp | **Inherited from M3-09 and measured here rather than assumed.** `crates/tunnel-acp-export` kills the child's process group with `rustix` on every end of life, which reaches a `/bin/sh` wrapper's grandchild — confirmed twice by reading the process table. It does **not** reach a descendant that calls `setsid`, calls `setpgid` or double-forks. `crates/tunnel-acp-fixture`'s `detached` mode calls `setsid` and records whether it succeeded; in the measured run on macOS the marker said `ok`, one group `SIGKILL` was recorded, and 500 ms later the process table showed the descendant **alive, in its own process group, and not a zombie**. The test is `a_descendant_that_calls_setsid_survives_the_process_group_kill` in `crates/tunnel-acp-fixture/tests/supervisor.rs`; a red there leads straight to this row. It asserts the **mechanism**, not only the outcome, because `kill -0` succeeds on an unreaped corpse: a descendant that a future containment really did kill but that nobody had reaped yet would otherwise read as "survived" and keep the test green for the wrong reason. It must be outside the child's process group and in a state that is not `Z`, so what is proven is that it survived *because* it left the group. 500 ms is generous in the safe direction: `SIGKILL` to a group member takes effect immediately, so a slow machine makes survival harder to observe, not easier. Group signalling is Unix-only and macOS is the only host any of this has run on, so nothing is known about Linux or Windows. **A sibling gap, named here rather than left implicit in a sentence: the device process itself dying.** On a `SIGKILL`, a `process::exit` or a crash of the CLI, **no `Drop` of any kind runs** — not the supervisor's, not the child handle's. The child then sees stdin at end of file and exits on its own, but nobody signals its process group, so a wrapper's grandchild is orphaned exactly as an escaping descendant is. This is not closable from inside the process, which is why the code's claim is now "every end **the supervisor lives to see**" rather than "every end of a child's life". It needs either a kernel-side parent-death facility (Linux has `PR_SET_PDEATHSIG`; **macOS has no equivalent**, and macOS is the only host here) or the same containment boundary the escaping descendant needs — which is why it belongs on this row and not on one of its own. It is **not** covered by any test in this chunk.<br><br>**Acceptance:** either adopt a containment boundary that survives `setsid` (a per-connection sandbox, container or VM profile, as `docs/acp.md`'s process policy already requires before any confinement is claimed), or state in the shipped documentation that an ACP agent's detaching descendants — and every descendant at all, if the device process is killed — are not cleaned up, and reconcile with M3-09 so the two are one decision rather than two rediscoveries. Both routes out of the group must be answered together: a fix for one that leaves the other open would let this row be closed while the hole stays open.<br><br>**M3-09 has now decided both halves, and this row inherits that decision rather than making it again.** The sibling gap named above — the device process itself dying — is **closed for the MCP stdio export and not yet for this one**: `crates/tunnel-deadman` gives each supervised child a parent-death sentinel holding the read end of a pipe the device holds the write end of, so a `SIGKILL` of the device closes the descriptor, the sentinel wakes on end of file and signals the group. It is portable to any Unix and needs no `PR_SET_PDEATHSIG`, which is what this row correctly said macOS does not have. Wiring it in here is a small change to `crates/tunnel-acp-export/src/child.rs`, where the group kill already lives, and it is **not** done by M3-09's chunk — it is the remaining work on this row's second half. The **first** half, the escaping descendant, stays open on macOS and is now measured on both sides. M3-09's fixture detaches by `setsid` **and** by a double fork, and **both survive with the sentinel armed**, because a sentinel sends the same group signal from a different process and therefore has the same reach. That is the answer to the tempting mistake this pair of rows invites: a deadman inverts *who* sends the signal, never *what it can touch*. The reach fix is a kernel boundary — cgroup v2 on Linux, a job object on Windows, nothing in-process on macOS — exactly as this row's acceptance already says, and `docs/mcp.md` now states it in shipped documentation. So the two rows are one decision: **trigger inverted everywhere, reach recorded as absent on macOS.** This row closes when the sentinel is wired into the ACP supervisor and `docs/acp.md` carries the statement `docs/mcp.md` now carries.<br><br>**Both are now done, and this closes on the trigger half only — the reach half is closed by the acceptance's *second* branch, a statement in shipped documentation, not by a mechanism.** `crates/tunnel-acp-export/src/child.rs` arms a `tunnel_deadman::Deadman` per child, immediately after the spawn, and stands it down only after the leader is killed and reaped. **The ordering guards a crash window, not pid reuse**, and the code says so: a stood-down sentinel never signals at all (`watch` returns `EXIT_STOOD_DOWN` before `kill_group`), so no ordering of an orderly stand-down can fire against any id; what an early stand-down would do is leave the group alive and **no longer watched**, and a `SIGKILL` inside that interval leaks it. It is a **stated trade**: on the token-failure path (the write fails, stdin is gone, the sentinel sees a bare end of file and fires) the late ordering is the *exposed* one, so the reuse race M3-18 carries mildly argues the other way. That is written in `child.rs`, not only here.<br><br>**Evidence, at pid level, in `crates/tunnel-acp-fixture/tests/process_residue.rs` (5 tests, all green).** The supervisor is a **separate process** — the fixture's new `supervise` mode, which runs a real `child::spawn` supervisor over an `npx`-shaped `wrapper` and parks — because a `SIGKILL` runs no `Drop`, no `kill_on_drop` and no handler and **cannot be simulated from inside the process holding the handle**. `a_sigkilled_supervisor_still_kills_the_group`: probe 51073, wrapper 51074, in-group helper 51076; after `kill -9` of the probe the helper's row is **`None`** — absent from the process table, not merely detached from a closed handle. **Control 1, that the fixture genuinely escapes the old mechanism:** `without_a_sentinel_a_sigkilled_supervisor_leaks_its_childs_group` runs the identical probe with the sentinel path naming no file (the state of `origin/main`), reports `armed=0`, and 500 ms after the `SIGKILL` the helper 51099 is **`Some(("51098", "S"))`** — alive, not a zombie, inside the very process group nobody signalled. The two differ in one respect and reach opposite outcomes. **Control 2, that an in-group helper is reachable at all:** `the_group_kill_reaches_an_in_group_helper` kills the same shape on the orderly path and its row goes to `None`, so "containment" is not claimed for something nothing could ever have contained. **The reach, re-measured with the sentinel armed:** `a_setsid_descendant_escapes_even_with_the_sentinel_armed` — descendant 51070, `setsid` marker `"ok"`, child group 51068, group kills 1, **sentinels armed 1**, and 500 ms later the descendant is `Some(("51070","Ss"))`: alive, state not `Z`, in a group of its own. Note the interaction that makes this awkward rather than merely undone: a key change arrives *through a membership record*, and a new record version invalidates every peer admission anyway (M7-C80), so a naive attempt would measure M7-C80's teardown and not the key change's. **Acceptance:** drive a staged key overlap — the shape `verify-m7-membership-hint-drop` already uses, where the old key leaves the verifier without a version bump doing the work — against a live ACP stream, and establish which of the two mechanisms tears it down, or record that they are indistinguishable from the stream's side. <br><br>**Closed by M8 chunk 7, and the acceptance's second half — "or record that they are indistinguishable from the stream's side" — turned out to be the true one, with a third answer beside it.** `verify-m8-acp-cluster` gains a `peer-key-rotation` case that stages the overlap (the owner's record approving the old key and an incoming key together, converged in **every** relay's verifier before anything is measured) and then runs the same sequence twice against a live ACP SSE stream on the non-owner ingress. The **control arm** publishes a byte-identical key list at a strictly newer version — same SPKIs, same key ids, same `not_before`/`expires_at`, the ids derived from the SPKI rather than from the version precisely so the two records' key lists cannot differ — so only `record_version` moves. The **key arm** drops the old key. **From the stream's side they are indistinguishable**: both produce an explicit interruption, neither produces a `stopReason`, and no code on the wire names a key — both answer a later admission `503 PEER_UNTRUSTED` / `not_dispatched`. **The product distinguishes them, and says so.** `RuntimeState::revalidate_active` reaches for `PeerInvalidationReason::MembershipRevoked` when and only when `bind_peer` **fails** for that admission, and for `MembershipChanged` when the binding still verifies and only the version moved. Observed, every run: control `["membership_changed"]`, key `["membership_revoked"]`. So the interruption **is** attributable to the key event, by the product's own recorded reason, with the control arm there to stop that reason being read as a coincidence of timing. **Where that attribution is not available.** `PeerInvalidationReason` has no string form, no serialization, no counter and no tracing field; it is a `u8` latched first-writer-wins on the admission's cancellation token. The only channel out is `MembershipRuntime::set_invalidation_callback`, so the gate records there — chaining the fixture's own `publish_verified_pins` and its M7-C81 pending latch, so installing the recorder changes what the fixture *records* and nothing about what it *does*. **The attribution is in-process and a consumer cannot make it**, which the gate's `NOT_COVERED` carries. **What is not claimed**: not that an ACP stream survives a key rotation (it does not, and the case asserts the teardown), and not that the key change was separated from the version bump *on the wire* — the verifier refuses an equal-version re-sign (`MembershipError::EqualVersionConflict`), so every key change is also a version change and no test can remove that. **The acceptance is met narrowly, and review had to say how narrowly.** The withdrawn key is the **owner's own serving key** and `INCOMING_SPKI` is a phantom no certificate presents, so the key arm also drives the owner's runtime through `MembershipRejected` to Unready, invalidating its own admission of the ingress at the same moment. The key arm is therefore **three concurrent teardowns** -- ingress-side revalidation, owner-side fail-closed, and the version bump -- and the control arm controls for the third only. **What is established is the ingress's own attribution of its own teardown**, cleanly separated from a version bump; **which end closed the socket first is not established**, and the first draft of this row's closure implied it was. Both ends' latched reasons are now recorded and asserted -- control `owner_reasons=[] owner_unready=false`, key `owner_reasons=["membership_revoked"] owner_unready=true` in all fourteen runs -- and a rule makes the disclosure load-bearing, so a fixture that later re-keys properly reddens the run instead of letting these paragraphs go stale. **A genuine rotation needs a fixture relay that really re-keys**, and this fixture cannot stage one: the admission under test binds the SPKI the owner actually presents, so withdrawing that SPKI and unreadying the owner are the same act. One staged instant now threads through every record in both arms, so the claim is true rather than nearly true. And "`MembershipRevoked` when and only when `bind_peer` fails" was overstated -- it is also the reason for `install_unready_candidate` and `mark_unready`, excluded here only because convergence on the ingress's verifier is observed first -- so the reason rules are pinned as **exact sets** rather than "contains".<br><br>**A defect found while building it**: `MembershipRecord` orders relay keys by activation and then by key id, so a key list assembled in the caller's argument order is refused `RelayKeysUnordered` and the membership runtime fails closed until it recovers. The case sorts by key id, which is also what lets the id be derived from the SPKI. `verify-m7-membership-hint-drop` never met this because its ids carry an index. | M8-C25 | [x] The ACP watchdog re-counts an expired session's subscription window on every tick, so `session_subscribe_expired` counts ticks, not expiries. | verified local | m8c10 worker (found by the m8c9 verification pass) | **Found by the m8c9 pass re-running M8-04's chain at `135ef8c`, and it is what stopped that row being promoted.** `cargo test --workspace --locked -- --test-threads=4` failed on its first run with `a_session_whose_subscriber_never_arrives_closes_its_window` (`crates/tunnel-acp-fixture/tests/bridge.rs`) red; a second run at the same revision was **1,793 passed, 0 failed, 55 ignored across 126 binaries**, the recorded figure exactly. Isolated, the test is red **3 of 12** runs on a machine at load average 7-8.<br><br>**It is not M8-C12's cause, and M8-C12's own guard rules that cause out.** M8-C12 diagnosed the same test reddening under load as the **connection** GET missing the shared `subscribe_ms` window, fixed it by raising that test's bound to 5000 ms, and added `assert_eq!(diagnostics.connection_subscribe_expired, 0)` so a recurrence would fail by name. That assertion **passes** in every failure observed here. The failing assertion is the next one, `session_subscribe_expired == 1`, against an observed **1,397, 1,401 and 1,421**. So this is a second, independent cause, and M8-C12's acceptance -- "fix the shared bound so the suite's own crates have no random reds" -- is still not met.<br><br>**The defect, in product code.** In `watchdog` (`crates/tunnel-acp-export/src/bridge.rs`) the **connection** branch expires the connection, publishes `last_expiry_elapsed_us`/`last_expiry_bound_us`, increments `connection_subscribe_expired`, calls `export.remove` and **returns** -- so it fires exactly once by construction. The **session** branch, immediately below, collects `state.sessions` values matching `!target.is_subscribed() && target.created.elapsed() > bound`, publishes the same two measurements, increments `session_subscribe_expired`, and calls `target.close()`. **`Target::close()` sets `closed` and takes the receiving half; it does not set `subscribed`, and it does not remove the target from `state.sessions`.** The filter therefore matches the same target again on the next `WATCHDOG_TICK` (20 ms) and on every tick after it, for the life of the connection. 1,397-1,421 is 28-29 s of ticks, which is the test's own 30 s polling window.<br><br>**What that falsifies.** `session_subscribe_expired` is named as, and asserted by its own test as, a count of sessions whose subscription window closed; it is in fact a count of **watchdog ticks since the first such closure**, and any figure quoted from it means something other than what it says. `last_expiry_elapsed_us` and `last_expiry_bound_us` are rewritten every 20 ms after the first expiry, so the pair a reader samples is of an arbitrary later tick, not of the expiry -- which defeats the ordering the code comments carefully establish ("the measurement is published before the counter that makes it findable"). And the test's `== 1` is a race that only a sample taken inside the first tick after expiry can win, which is why it is red about a quarter of the time rather than always. **Nothing observable is wrong with the closing itself**: the window does close, the target is closed once, and the late session GET is still refused 409 -- the test's own later assertions pass when it gets that far.<br><br>**Acceptance.** Make the sweep idempotent at its source: exclude an already-closed target from the filter (`!target.is_closed()`), so the counter counts **expiries**. **Do not** instead drop the expired target from `state.sessions` — an earlier draft of this acceptance offered the two as equivalent and review showed they are not. Removing it makes the late session GET fall through `session_target` to `None` and answer **404 instead of 409**, which breaks this test's own final assertion and contradicts M8-02's recorded claim that the same mechanism keeps an expired session's window closed. The `is_closed()` form masks nothing: a never-subscribed target's receiver is parked until `close()` takes it, so a send cannot fail on it first, and `established_and_broken` already excludes closed targets — the sweep simply becomes consistent with the rule beside it. Keep the publish-before-count ordering. **Also record what this defect says about every figure taken over this suite:** the sweep is unchanged since `b4bea95` (chunk 3) and M8-C12's stabilisation never touched it, so the single-run `1,793 passed / 0 failed` figures the m8c6 and m8c8 passes each recorded were **one sample from a suite already red roughly one run in five on this test**. That is precisely the tally-where-a-rate-is-needed shape M8-C12 exists to forbid, and it went unnoticed because the sample happened to be green. Then make the once-only property **load-bearing** rather than incidental -- a falsification and a guard case in the ACP guard suite, so a future change that reintroduces the re-count reddens something by name. **Do not raise the test's bound again**: M8-C12 already raised it from 300 ms to 1500 ms to 5000 ms, and this failure is at 5000 ms with the connection window demonstrably untouched; a bound tuned until a run passes is what this repository distrusts, and here it would hide the defect rather than fix it.<br><br>**Consequence for every guard figure, which is M8-C12's warning arriving a second time.** `scripts/acp-guard-deletion.py` counts a mutated case as guarded when a test reddens. A random red landing on a case whose guard is not load-bearing is **silent** and is counted as a red, so a guard that protects nothing is recorded as protecting something. The `m8c4` suite runs the crates this test lives in, so its figures are the exposed ones; `m8c5` runs the harness's own library tests and is not. Re-run `--suite m8c4` after the fix before any figure from it is quoted again. —<br><br>**Implemented at `7808ea7` on `m8c10-watchdog`, awaiting verification.** The sweep's filter now reads `!target.is_subscribed() && !target.is_closed() && target.created.elapsed() > bound`; `Target::close()` is unchanged and the target **stays in `state.sessions`**, so the late session GET still finds a closed target and is refused **409**, not 404. The publish-before-count ordering is unchanged.<br><br>**Red then green, measured, not tallied.** Isolated runs of `a_session_whose_subscriber_never_arrives_closes_its_window` at `7808ea7` before the fix: **4 red of 16**, observed `session_subscribe_expired` of **1376, 1370, 1371, 1387** against `== 1`; red runs took 32-33 s (the whole 30 s poll window) and green runs 5 s. After the fix: **0 red of 16. **And the stronger argument is structural, not statistical — review supplied it.** 0 of 16 plus eight green workspace runs against a ~1-in-4 rate excludes "unchanged" at about 0.1%, but it does not by itself exclude "rarer". What excludes "rarer" is the code: `closed` is written `true` at exactly one site and **never reset**, and `state.sessions` is never removed from or re-inserted except through `entry().or_insert_with`, so a given `Target` can satisfy `!is_closed()` in the sweep **at most once**. The once-only property is now an invariant of a monotone flag rather than a property of timing, which is why this is fixed and not merely made rare**, every run 5 s. `cargo test --workspace --locked -- --test-threads=4` was run **eight times** after the fix: **1,794 passed, 0 failed, 55 ignored across 126 binaries** on every run (1,794, not 1,793, because of the new test below). **Eight runs is the point**: the figure this row exists to discredit was a single run.<br><br>**The once-only property is now load-bearing.** `an_expired_session_window_is_counted_once_not_once_per_watchdog_tick` (`crates/tunnel-acp-fixture/tests/bridge.rs`) waits for the expiry, lets **twenty-five further 20 ms ticks** pass, and asserts `session_subscribe_expired` is still 1 **and** that `last_expiry_elapsed_us` / `last_expiry_bound_us` are unchanged -- the half of the defect that no assertion reached at all. Its message "counted once per expiry, not once per watchdog tick" is unique to the rule. Deleting only the `!target.is_closed()` term reddens it **5 of 5** isolated runs (observed 26, 26, 26, 2, 26), so the guard is deterministic where the old test was a race. **The `2` is not an outlier and is worth naming:** that run reddened at the *pre-wait* assertion ("the first observation of the expiry is a single expiry") because the first sample landed after the second tick, not at the post-wait one. So the falsification reddens through **two different messages**, and the claim that the case's message is unique to the rule covers only the post-wait one. Review caught this; 26 is the expected value (1 + 25 ticks). The matching `m8c3` guard case is "an expired session window is counted once, not once per watchdog tick", and `docs/acp.md` carries the falsification beside the subscription-deadline bullet. | M8-C28 | [x] A relay binds one serving identity for the life of its process, so no peer-key rotation can keep the rotating relay `Ready`. | verified local | unassigned (found by the m8c13 worker) | **Found by trying to build M8-C24's re-keying fixture relay and discovering the blocker is in the product.** M8-C24 asks the cluster fixture for "a relay that genuinely re-keys -- generating a second serving certificate and switching the identity it presents". The first half is a fixture matter and is easy (`FixturePki::issue_peer` mints a second certificate for the same `node_id`). **The second half is not implementable at any layer above the relay.**<br><br>**The mechanism, exactly.** `crates/tunnel-relay/src/main.rs` reads `cluster.peer_tls_cert_chain` **once** at startup and derives `local_spki` from the first certificate. `MembershipRuntimeConfig::with_local_spki_sha256` (`crates/tunnel-relay/src/membership_runtime.rs`) stores that digest in a single `Option<String>` through a **consuming builder that has no setter**. Readiness then requires the reconciled record to contain **exactly that one SPKI**, un-revoked, with `not_before <= now <= expires_at`; the `local_key` lookup takes the local pin rather than `active_key` precisely so an unrelated newer key cannot stand in as this process's identity proof. Miss it and the runtime takes `MembershipUnreadyReason::MembershipRejected`, goes **Unready**, and latches `PeerInvalidationReason::MembershipRevoked` against its own admissions. The in-process fixture path is identical -- `ServeConfig::start_with_peer` receives a `PeerListenerConfig` once. A repository-wide search finds **no reload, no re-key, no second local SPKI and no setter** in `tunnel-relay`.<br><br>**The asymmetry this exposes.** The product already supports a key overlap on the **verifying** side: a membership record may approve an outgoing and an incoming key together, and `verify-m7-membership-hint-drop` drives exactly that. It supports **no overlap on the serving side** -- a relay cannot present key B while still being recognised under key A. A staged rotation therefore has no interval in which the successor *serves* and the rotating relay is still `Ready`, which is the interval a rotation **is**.<br><br>**Consequences, which are larger than one gate.** (1) M8-C24's acceptance is unreachable and that row is blocked on this one. (2) M8-05's first discriminator -- the owner stays `Ready` through a rotation with a serving successor -- **cannot be proven by any test** until this lands, and that is a statement about the product rather than about the harness. (3) Operationally this says a deployment cannot rotate a relay's peer key without that relay failing closed and invalidating its admissions; whether that is acceptable is an owner decision this row surfaces rather than settles. Restarting the relay with the new certificate is **not** a rotation: the restart is owner loss, its own teardown, and any interruption would be attributable to it rather than to the key event.<br><br>**The obvious workaround does not work either, and it is closed here so "cannot be proven by any test" is airtight.** A reader will propose running a **second concurrent relay process for the same `node_id`**, presenting key B, while process A still presents key A -- giving a serving overlap without any product change. It fails for the same reason, one layer out: a membership record carries **one `peer_endpoint` per node**, so only one of the two is dialable as that identity, and the ACP stream under test is already riding **process A's** admission. When A's SPKI leaves the record, A takes `MembershipRejected` and self-revokes exactly as before -- the second process changes which endpoint a *new* dial reaches and nothing about the teardown being measured. The same objection answers a second `node_id`: that is a different peer, not a rotation of this one.<br><br>**Acceptance:** let a relay hold **more than one local serving identity** during a bounded overlap -- at minimum, readiness satisfied by *any* non-revoked, in-window record key whose SPKI the relay can present, with the presented certificate selectable so a successor can begin serving while the predecessor is still approved. Then M8-C24's gate work becomes possible: stage the overlap, switch the served identity, withdraw the old key, and assert the owner stays `Ready` throughout while the ingress still attributes its teardown to the key. Neither the scope of the change nor its security review is settled here; the row exists so the requirement is tracked against the product rather than left as a fixture limitation, which is how M8-C16 mislaid it once already.<br><br>**2026-09-26: implemented as M8-C45.** A relay now holds a replaceable serving identity. Readiness is bound to the served key; switching is gated on the verified record approving the successor; the predecessor drains and is retired, with no restart. This row closes with M8-C45.<br><br>**Verification sweep (M8 sweep, 2026-09-26T18:38:08+10:00) at `343fd3fd`: stays open with M8-C45, on M8-C60.** The product change exists, and the process gate passed at this head. The ACP-level proof that a re-keying relay stays Ready is the genuine case, and that case has one unexplained failure in 15 (M8-C60).<br><br>**Merged-head re-test (M8 sweep, 2026-09-26T20:24:10+10:00): promoted with M8-C45.** A relay now holds a replaceable serving identity. Readiness is bound to the served key and satisfied by it during the overlap, and the successor can be selected while the predecessor is still approved. That is shown end to end in 40 of 40 genuine rotations at `b649fcca` and `0df4dc25`, with the rotating owner never Unready. It is shown for a configured `tunnel-relay serve` process by `m8_relay_rekey_process` at `0df4dc25` (`m8-harness-1597.log`; the `b649fcca` run is discarded, see M8-C45). See M8-C45. | 2026-09-26T20:24:10+10:00 |
| M8-C29 | [ ] Bound or close the parent-death sentinel's arming window. | planned | acp (found in M8-C07) | **Named rather than left to be rediscovered, and it is the last uncovered gap in M8-C07's trigger half.** A sentinel can only watch a pid that exists, so `crates/tunnel-acp-export/src/child.rs` arms it on the line after `Command::spawn` returns — and `crates/tunnel-mcp-export/src/child.rs` has the identical shape. Between those two points the child's process group **exists and is unwatched**: a `SIGKILL`, a `process::exit` or a crash of the device in that interval leaks the group exactly as it did before either chunk. The code says so rather than claiming zero ("it is microseconds and cannot be closed without arming the sentinel before the pid it watches exists, but it is not zero and is not claimed to be"), and this row is where that statement is tracked. **Why it is not simply closable by moving the line:** the sentinel takes the leader's pid as an argument, so arming first needs either a pid that does not yet exist or a second round trip in which the supervisor tells an already-running sentinel which group to watch — and that hand-off has a window of its own, in the other direction, where a sentinel is armed against nothing and a crash before the hand-off leaves the *child* unwatched anyway. **It is also not measured.** No test here brackets the window, and a test that did would have to win a race it cannot schedule; the honest statement is that the bound is unknown, not that it is small. **Options:** arm the sentinel *before* the spawn and hand it the pid over its own pipe, accepting the mirrored window and measuring which is narrower; have the sentinel itself spawn the child, so there is no window at all but the supervisor loses the handle it reaps with; or adopt the kernel boundary M3-09 and M8-C07 both record, which makes the question disappear along with the reach hole. **Acceptance:** either a mechanism with no unwatched interval, or a measured bound on the window with the reasoning written down — the same acceptance shape M3-18 carries for the reuse race, and for the same reason: "vanishingly small" is a measurement nobody has taken. | — |

| M8-C45 | [x] A relay re-keys its private HTTP/3 peer identity without a restart: stage, switch after a continuous signed approval, drain, retire. | verified local | relay-rekey worker | **The product change M8-C28 asked for.** `tunnel_transport::RotatingPeerIdentity` is one replaceable identity slot behind the relay's peer listener *and* its outbound peer client (a rustls `ResolvesServerCert`/`ResolvesClientCert` pair), so an install changes what **new** handshakes present in both directions and never an established connection. `MembershipRuntime` now binds readiness to the **served** SPKI (`local_serving_spki`), changed only by `switch_local_serving_spki`, which holds the reconcile gate and refuses unless the verified record approves the key at that instant; a staged or merely approved key never satisfies readiness, so a relay whose served key is withdrawn still fails closed. `tunnel_relay::peer_rekey::PeerRekey` is the explicit stage → switch → overlap → retire state machine; `PeerClient::with_local_identity` moves pooled outbound connections under a superseded identity into a drain set bounded at `MAX_ROTATION_DRAINING_CONNECTIONS` (4). Private keys stay in process memory; Redis carries only the publisher's signed approval. Design: [cluster.md](cluster.md#certificate-and-key-lifecycle).<br><br>**Evidence so far (local, macOS):** `crates/tunnel-transport/tests/m8_peer_identity_rotation.rs` 5/5 over real QUIC/TLS; `crates/tunnel-relay/tests/m7_readiness.rs` `m8c45_*` 3/3 and `rekey::*` 3/3; each new test shown red under a named mutation (logs `red-transport-drain.log`, `red-membership-switch.log`, `red-rekey-machine.log`). The `server install` test has no pre-fix form to go red against: before this row there was no install API at all. **Open:** the end-to-end gates on M8-C24 and M8-C46 must pass before this row closes.<br><br>**Review of PR #183 (2026-09-26), all fixed at `7f860ded`/`a927bcb9`:** an explicit `Switching` phase, so a trigger mid-switch is refused rather than lost. The bound (`SEQUENTIAL_JOURNAL_ENTRY_BOUND = 2`, "observed: 1") assumes the entry of request *k* is reclaimed before request *k+2* is admitted. The connector releases an entry only once the owner's `STREAM_FORGET` for it has completed its carrier barriers, and the owner forgets only after the connector's cumulative ACK has reached its FIN ([protocol.md](protocol.md#open-retry-horizon-and-journal-reclamation)), so the lag is set by ACK and barrier cadence against the request rate, which differ by host; nothing found in the code bounds it at one request. **Deliberately not relaxed:** raising the bound would be lowering a floor on evidence of one environment. **Acceptance:** decide from the reclamation path whether a peak of 3 is legitimate (and then derive the bound rather than tune it) or a defect; the failing run now prints its evidence (362977c). **CI decision:** because of this row the M3 job is not added to `ci.yml`; see M3-25.<br><br>**Explained on branch `m3-features` (b260799, corrected at df91cb9 after the Opus review of 50c5c34; see the correction below): no leak was found. The owner publishes `STREAM_FORGET` only when `flush_owner_stream_forgets` runs: after an inbound frame on the session, a reset, an OPENED or REJECTED, or the 500 ms maintenance tick. The owner's `CloseEchoStream` command never called it, and that command is usually the event that makes an HTTP stream's FORGET provable: the connector's FIN, carrying its ACK of the owner's FIN, arrives while the exchange task is still finishing, and the stream becomes terminal only at the close. So request *k*'s FORGET waited for request *k+1*'s frames. If the owner's close of *k* ran after them, it waited for *k+2*'s frames, and that gives a third entry at the sample. A slower host loses that race more often. **Fix:** the close command now flushes owner forgets under the same rules, including the rotation-freeze serialization. If the stream still owes a deferred ACK or window update, it also waits for the next 100 ms deadline poll. Meanwhile the consumer already has its response. Nothing orders entry *k*'s release before request *k+2*'s admission ([protocol.md](protocol.md#open-retry-horizon-and-journal-reclamation) now says so). The gate now requires the journal's **entry count** to return to its pre-loop value once all 160 streams have retired (rule `the OPEN journal returned to its starting size once every sequential stream retired`, mutation `journal leak`). That is read from the count itself, independently of the exact `open_streams_retired` rule, and a single leaked entry fails it, which the peak rule never guaranteed. The peak is still printed. **Measured after the fix:** local peak 1, before 0, after 0 in 3 of 3 runs (1 or 2 before the fix). The pre-fix hosted peak of 3 is *consistent with* that leftover plus two sequential entries, but no pre-fix run printed its starting count, so that is an inference. **CI:** the `m3-acceptance` job is added to `.github/workflows/ci.yml` (b260799): Linux with a Redis service, running `scripts/m3-harness-verify.sh`, with no artifacts and no process-log directories (M7-C112). `scripts/m3-harness-verify.sh` passed **3 of 3** consecutive local runs at `b260799` (nonces `m3f-m3hv-final1-1790277249-2848`, `m3f-m3hv-final2-1790277564-3532`, `m3f-m3hv-final3-1790277856-4078`; the tree differed from `b260799` only in docs for the last two), and **10 of 10** suite runs on hosted Linux in probe run 36046720180 (five jobs of two runs each, on branch `ci-m3-probe2`, whose one commit on top of `b260799` changed only `ci.yml` to run the M3 job that way; branch since deleted, no artifacts).<br><br>**Correction (Opus review of `50c5c34`).** The measurement recorded above as "hosted peak 2, before 1, after 1" did not show what it was cited for. Both passed "retired exactly +160" and `after <= before`. **Fixed and measured (840b91a, df91cb9).** The connector's status now names the retained entries (`open_journal_stream_ids`, bounded, identifiers only). The gate waits up to 15 s for the earlier phases' entries to be reclaimed, and requires that baseline to be **zero** (rule `the earlier phases' OPEN journal entries were all reclaimed`). | M3-32 | [x] Decide how the ingress records a consumer release after the final SSE response but before END. | verified local | m3-features worker (found by the m3-reliability worker; raised by the Opus review of `ba86d10`) | **Split out of M3-23.** rmcp 3.4.0's client drops a POST's SSE stream 50 ms after the final JSON-RPC response (`execute_sse_stream`, `close_on_response`). The device's END and FIN reach the ingress after the final event's bytes, so whenever they take longer than 50 ms the ingress's `ChannelBody` is dropped with its unknown-length body still open, and the ingress records `HTTP_CANCELLED` for an MCP call the consumer received in full. That is accurate about the transport and false about the call's outcome. It is routine, not a race at the margin: an idle run of `verify-m3-mcp-cloud-client` drained 25 such streams across 28 cases, and the gate hides it only because its client reads the stream on (M3-23's `DrainAfterResponse`). **Acceptance:** decide whether a release after the final SSE response and before END is a consumer cancellation, a completed exchange, or a third recorded outcome -- the MCP profile knows when the final response has been sent, the generic HTTP bridge does not -- and pin the decision with a test that drops the body in that window without the gate's drain.<br><br>**Decided and implemented on branch `m3-features` (c3a6083): a third recorded outcome, `released`.** The docs determine it. The relay validates heads only and never interprets bodies ([mcp.md](mcp.md), Dispatch policy), so the ingress cannot tell a release after the final JSON-RPC response from one in the middle of a call. Recording `complete` would claim a call outcome the ingress cannot know, and recording an ordinary `aborted` is what this row calls false. AGENTS.md's explicit-ambiguous-outcome rule therefore gives a transport-true third outcome: *the consumer released the response body after its head; the call's outcome is the device's record* -- authoritative for the call exactly as the device's dispatch record is for `execution`. `tunnel_http_bridge::Outcome::Released` (response direction only) is recorded when the consumer goes away after the head was committed; before the head it is still an ordinary `aborted` cancellation. **Nothing on the wire changes:** the same RESET with `HTTP_CANCELLED` is sent, so a 2026 handler still running is cancelled, and a 2026 stdio child that already answered gets no `notifications/cancelled` because its request guard had completed. The relay records it as `response_outcome: "released"`. **Pinned without the gate's drain:** `a_release_after_the_final_event_and_before_end_is_recorded_as_released` (tunnel-http-bridge `streaming.rs`). The device sends an interim and a final SSE event, then END and FIN, which a relay in the test holds back. The consumer reads the whole call and drops the body, and only then are END and FIN released. The ingress records `released`, `HTTP_CANCELLED`, `dispatched`; the device records `complete` with no error. The other half is `consumer_drop_mid_body_resets_both_directions_and_the_handler_observes_it`: a mid-stream release is also `released` at the ingress, and there the device records `aborted` with `HTTP_CANCELLED`. The real-path gate's cancel case now requires `released` at the ingress beside the device's `aborted` (rule `cancelled ingress response released`). **Red** with `consumer_left` reverted to the old abort: both tests fail `left: Aborted, right: Released` (nonce `m3f-red-m332-1790275675-94242`), and the new guard case `m3c32-release` in `scripts/m3-guard-deletion.py` reproduces it (nonce `m3f-guard-m3c32-1790276150-97501`). **Kept:** the cloud-client gate's post-response drain (M3-23), because its streaming rule still requires no ingress error and a released exchange still carries `HTTP_CANCELLED`. `scripts/m3-harness-verify.sh` passed **3 of 3** consecutive local runs at `b260799` (nonces `m3f-m3hv-final1-1790277249-2848`, `m3f-m3hv-final2-1790277564-3532`, `m3f-m3hv-final3-1790277856-4078`; the tree differed from `b260799` only in docs for the last two), and **10 of 10** suite runs on hosted Linux in probe run 36046720180 (five jobs of two runs each, on branch `ci-m3-probe2`, whose one commit on top of `b260799` changed only `ci.yml` to run the M3 job that way; branch since deleted, no artifacts).<br><br>**Review fix (Opus review of `50c5c34`, df91cb9).** `commit` set `committed` before handing the head over and ignored a failed send. So a consumer that dropped the pending head at that instant was recorded as `released` for a head it never received. Now `commit` clears `committed` when the send fails, and holds the head lock from the store until it knows the outcome. `consumer_left` reads `committed` under the same lock, so it never sees the transient value. Unit tests in `tunnel-http-bridge` `owner.rs`: `a_head_the_consumer_never_took_is_not_a_release` and `a_head_the_consumer_took_makes_leaving_a_release`. **Red** without the clear: `left: Released, right: Aborted` (nonce `m3f-red-m332-race-1790279744-22819`). Guard suite `m3c32-release-race` is RED on its declared witness (`m3f-guard-race-1790280046-24048`). `verify-m8-acp-cluster`'s revocation check now counts `released` ingress records as well as `aborted` ones, so a release cannot hide a withdrawn exchange there. `scripts/m3-harness-verify.sh` passed 2 of 2 local runs at `df91cb9` (nonces `m3f-m3hv-review1-1790280067-24385`, `m3f-m3hv-review2-1790280386-25704`; the second with only docs and site edits in the tree), and `verify-m8-acp-cluster` passed once there (`m3f-acp-cluster-1790280672-26766`). | 2026-09-25T06:14:43+10:00 |

| M5-C08 | [x] Supervise the CUA backend: lifecycle, a health probe that is not a config echo, and a restart that cannot double-dispatch. | implemented (verified local) | m5c4 worker | **The owner's D4 decision, implemented: the device supervises the backend -- "ensures it's running and working" -- so lifecycle *and* health.** It inherits M3-09's and M8-C07's containment picture wholesale and does not overstate it.<br><br>**Lifecycle.** `crates/tunnel-cua-export/src/child.rs` starts the backend in its own process group, signals that group with `rustix` on every end of life this process lives to see, and arms a `tunnel_deadman::Deadman` per backend, stood down only after the leader is killed and reaped. The ordering guards a **crash window, not pid reuse**: a stood-down sentinel never signals at all (`watch` returns `EXIT_STOOD_DOWN` before `kill_group`), so no ordering of an orderly stand-down can fire against any id; what an early stand-down would do is leave the group alive and **no longer watched**. **A second, separate residue on the same theme, found by review and recorded rather than claimed away:** of the two `kill_group` calls, only the one on the kill branch is pre-reap. The one after the `select!` runs on both paths after `child.wait()` has reaped the leader, and on a natural exit it is the *only* group signal -- so it targets a group id that is a released pid and in principle recyclable. It is kept because dropping it would leave a naturally exited wrapper's helpers unsignalled, which is the case the group kill exists for; closing it properly wants a handle valid across the reap (`pidfd` on Linux) and **macOS has none**. The header's old blanket claim that the group "is signalled while the leader is still unreaped" has been narrowed to the branch where it is true. It is a **stated trade**: on the token-failure path -- the write fails because the pipe is already gone, so the sentinel sees a bare end of file and fires -- the late ordering is the *exposed* one, because the group has been reaped and its id may already be free. Renaming the constant -- the most obvious way to make the pin stop existing -- left the script printing `ok parameter pin: 14 allowlisted commands ... all matching` over a table it had never found, exit 0. Caught by running the rename as a red case rather than assuming the `find` worked; fixed by requiring the colon, after which the rename exits 1 with `COMMAND_PARAMETERS is not declared`. **It never landed**, which is the only thing separating it from the five above. *Seventh*: in the same chunk, `cargo test --workspace \| grep -E "^(error\|failures:)"` printed nothing and was briefly read as "no failures" -- a result indistinguishable from a grep whose pattern could not match the output. Replaced by writing the run to a file and tallying every `test result:` line, which reports the figure and so reports that it ran. The ordinal remains a running count, not a claim the list is complete.<br><br>**Closed at `f3ec519`. The criterion survived, and the figures reproduce verbatim.** Re-measured at `eb24220` in an empty `CARGO_TARGET_DIR`: `cargo test -p tunnel-cua -p tunnel-cua-fixture --locked` exits **101** with `test result: FAILED. 2 passed; 4 failed`, the same four test names. The absence of the helper was confirmed three ways rather than inferred -- `target/debug/tunnel-deadman` is missing after `--no-run`, after a `--test process_residue` run, and after the row's own unfiltered command -- and no build script or test in the selected packages builds it.<br><br>**One correction to this row, found by measurement.** It says all four print the warning and fail `armed == 1`. **Three do**: two at `process_residue.rs:229` through `measure_escape`, and one at `:519` whose `assert_eq!` carried **no message at all**, which is the weakest of the four. The fourth, `a_sigkilled_supervisor_still_kills_the_backends_group`, already failed with a *named* reason at `:89` -- `the sentinel binary must be built; run the workspace test command, not a bare -p run` -- because it resolved the path through a helper that asserted `is_file()`. So the pattern this row asks for already existed in the file for one of the four; the fix extends it to a skip for all four, because **a named refusal is still a red test that never ran**.<br><br>**What was built.** `sentinel_or_skip()`, keyed on the already-public `tunnel_deadman::availability()` -- no product API had to be invented. The four tests return early reporting `SKIPPED <name>: DID NOT RUN (SentinelMissing) -- ... This is a missing fixture, NOT a broken mechanism`, naming both the remedy and this row. The two surviving `armed` assertions now say that the caller's skip established the helper resolves, so a zero is the arming code regressing rather than an absent fixture. Not a `#[cfg]` guard, which this row records as rejected.<br><br>**The skip is itself guarded, which this row demands.** `the_skip_cannot_hide_a_helper_that_is_on_disk` compares the skip's own decision against `helper_is_on_disk()`, which reads the two candidate paths directly and **does not call `sentinel_path()`** -- so the two sides are computed independently and this is not an `assert_eq!` whose halves move together (M5-C10). **Its limit, stated so "independent" is not read too broadly:** the two sides are separately *written*, but they share `std::env::current_exe()` as an input. So the control catches "the skip reports the helper missing when it is there", which is the regression that would silently delete the coverage; it does **not** catch both sides agreeing to look in the wrong directory. It is reachable and falsifiable in both modes -- `false == false` package-scoped, `true == true` in a workspace run -- and prints the pair it measured, so a green result also reports that it ran. Both modes were measured: helper absent -> 7 passed, exit 0, every skip naming itself; helper built beside the tests -> 7 passed, exit 0, **zero** `DID NOT RUN` lines, `sentinels armed 1` in both escape measurements, and the control printing `helper on disk true, skip resolved it true`.<br><br>**Red-then-green from the harness, not by hand.** New suite `m5c8` in `scripts/m5-guard-deletion.py` defeats `availability()` into always reporting the helper missing -- the exact regression that would silently skip everything: `m5c8: 1 of 1 defeated guards turned a test red`, the named red being `the_skip_cannot_hide_a_helper_that_is_on_disk`. `C4_BUILD` is load-bearing for this suite rather than boilerplate: with no helper beside the tests the control correctly asserts `false == false` and the case would report `still green` over a rule that was never exercised.<br><br>**Eighth instance, appended by the m5c8 worker, and the interesting half is *where the binary came from*.** These four tests' result depends on a binary that **no target in the selected packages builds**, so a target directory that already holds a `tunnel-deadman` makes them pass. That is why this row's baseline was briefly unreproducible: the first baseline taken for this chunk was **green** (exit 0, 181 passed) in a `CARGO_TARGET_DIR` holding a `tunnel-deadman` linked at 12:08:15, while that same run's own fixture binary was linked at 12:46:48 -- so the helper was not built by that run's unit graph.<br><br>**Attributed, on review, to a shared target directory across two worktrees, which is the real defect here.** The `m5c7` worker's `guard.sh` exported the **same** `CARGO_TARGET_DIR` and then ran `scripts/m5-guard-deletion.py --suite m5c7` from a *different* worktree (`agent-a509e430fa9993289`, branch `m5c7-param-names`); its log's write window closes at 12:09:46, containing 12:08:15. Every `m5c4`-and-later suite carries `build=C4_BUILD` (`scripts/m5-guard-deletion.py:1165`) = `cargo build --locked -p tunnel-deadman -p tunnel-cua-fixture --bins`, which is the only command in play that links the helper binary. So the helper standing beside the tests had been **built from another worktree's source tree**. It happened to be a correct binary only because `m5c7` mutates `tunnel-http-forward` and `tunnel-cua*` rather than `tunnel-deadman` -- had the sibling been running the `m5c4` sentinel cases, the green baseline would have been measured against a *deliberately defeated* sentinel. **That is luck, not isolation**, and it is the per-worker `CARGO_TARGET_DIR` rule being crossed rather than merely a stale artefact. The generalisable form is worse than "a stale binary passed the test": **two worktrees silently sharing build output means one branch's guard mutation can be linked into another branch's measurement.**<br><br>**The method lesson, recorded because the first write-up got it wrong.** This was first filed as *unattributable*, with the reasoning that inventing a mechanism is how the previous chunk shipped a fabricated citation. Declining to invent was right; declining to **look** was not -- the evidence was three scripts away in the same scratchpad, in file mtimes and a sibling's log. So: before recording a gap as unattributable, exhaust the cheap local evidence, and treat "I could not attribute this" as a claim that itself needs a search behind it. The skip does not fix this instance -- a resident helper still makes the tests run for real -- but the control now prints which mode a run was in, so the ambiguity is at least visible in the output.<br><br>**Ninth instance, same worker.** `EXPECTED_GUARD_ANCHORS["m5-guard-deletion.py"]` in `scripts/test_guard_outcomes.py` stood at **82** while the harness checked **100**. That floor is a `>=` check whose whole job is to notice a scan that selected almost nothing, and one lagging 18 behind the truth could no longer notice an entire suite dropping out. Raised to the measured 100. A floor that is never re-measured decays into a check that cannot fail.<br><br>**Tenth instance, appended by the m6c1 worker (M6-04), and it is the first one on this list where the check that could not fail was a *positive control itself*.** M6-04's licence policy needed a control proving `deny.toml` fails closed, so the control narrowed the real allowlist -- deleting `"MIT"` -- and required cargo-deny to go red. It reported **PASS**. It was proving nothing: the command was `cargo-deny --offline --config <path> check licenses`, and this CLI accepts `--config` only *after* the subcommand, so cargo-deny exited **2** on `error: unexpected argument '--config' found` without resolving a single crate. The control asserted only `returncode != 0`, and a usage error satisfies that as neatly as a policy rejection does.<br><br>**What caught it was the control printing a figure it did not need to print.** Its message included `0 rejection records` next to the claim that the policy had rejected something, and those two cannot both be true. Corrected, the same control is `... check licenses --config <path>` and reports exit **4**, `licenses FAILED`, and **82** `error[rejected]` records. So the difference between the broken and the working control was visible only in a number that a narrower success message would have omitted -- which is the generalisable lesson and a stronger form of this row's own rule: it is not enough for a green to report *that* it ran, it has to report **how much it did**, because "exited non-zero" and "rejected 82 crates" look identical through a boolean.<br><br>**The fix is on the assertion, not just the argument order.** The control now requires a non-zero exit **and** at least one `error[rejected]` record **and** cargo-deny's own `licenses FAILED` verdict, and it detects `unexpected argument` / `Usage:` explicitly and reports *the control is broken* rather than passing. A red from the wrong cause is not evidence, and this is the shape that makes it look like evidence.<br><br>**One near-instance from the same chunk, recorded as *not* counted, because the distinction is the useful part.** The history scanner's `git cat-file --batch` reader opened the pipe with `bufsize=0`, whose `read(n)` is a single syscall that may return fewer bytes than asked for; a short read left the stream one object out of step. That **crashed loudly** (`ValueError` on a stray hash) and is therefore not a check that could not fail. It is noted only because the quieter variant is squarely on this list: a desynchronised reader that happened not to crash would have scanned shifted garbage while still reporting `4144 blobs scanned`, wearing the exact size of a scan that had covered everything. The reader now loops to the requested length, refuses a header that is not a `blob` record, and **reports the number of blobs it actually read back** rather than the number it intended to -- so the two figures diverging is visible instead of silent. The ordinal stays a running count, not a claim the list is complete.<br><br>**Eleventh instance, found by the Fable review of the m6c1 chunk, and it is the sharpest one on this list: the check that could not fail was a positive control, in the set of controls written to prevent exactly this.** M6-04's `deps` check carries a crate floor whose entire job is to notice a licence policy that examined nothing. Its control, `control_deps_empty_graph_would_not_pass`, asserted `CRATES_FLOOR > 0` and printed "361 measured at 6fad2fb" -- **a string literal**. Its docstring claimed it drove the floor comparison with a collapsed count; nothing was driven, no figure was measured, and a constant cannot drop below another constant. So the floor had no control while appearing in a list of ten as though it did, and the chunk's own report repeated the hard-coded 361 as though it were a measurement.<br><br>**Why it survived a chunk that was actively hunting this defect class**: it was written in the same pass that filed instance ten, and it *reads* like a control -- it has the name, the docstring, the tuple return, and a green line in the output. The tell was available and unread, the same tell as instance ten: the message quoted a number the code never computed. **A control that cannot name where its figure came from is the shape to distrust**, and that generalises past this file.<br><br>**Fixed by factoring the comparison into `crate_floor_verdict(examined)` and driving it four ways**: 0 must be rejected, `CRATES_FLOOR - 1` must be rejected, `CRATES_FLOOR` must be accepted, and **the live count from `cargo deny list` right now** must be accepted -- so if the workspace ever shrank below the floor the control goes red naming the real figure. Two neighbouring controls carried the same latent defect and were fixed with it: the shallow-clone control quoted "full depth: 779 commits, 4144 blobs" from memory beside a live figure, and the self-source control announced "15 patterns" after the set had grown to 18. Both now measure what they print.<br><br>**Twelfth instance, found by the Fable review of the same chunk, and it is in the control written to close the previous round's minor.** `control_working_tree_branch_is_scanned` was added because the working-tree branch had no control at all, and it claimed to test three cases: untracked, modified, and **renamed**. It wrote a one-line file, `git mv`d it, then **replaced the entire content** with the fixture and ran `git add -A`. Git's rename detection needs roughly 50% similarity, so `git status --porcelain` emitted `A renamed.toml` and `D to-rename.toml` and **never an `R ... -> ...` line at all**. The `" -> "` parsing branch was never entered, so reverting the parser fix left the control green over a mechanism it had not touched. `git add -A` also turned the "untracked" case into a staged `A` entry, so that half was untested too.<br><br>**Reproduced both ways before fixing, rather than taken on the reviewer's word** (the standing rule that a relayed mechanism is unmeasured until re-derived). Content fully replaced: `A renamed.toml` / `D to-rename.toml`, no rename. Content kept with the fixture appended and no `git add -A`: `RM to-rename.toml -> renamed.toml`.<br><br>**The tell was in the control's own output and went unread, for the third time in three rounds.** The scan printed `working tree: ... 1 skipped ... ['to-rename.toml']` -- a figure a real rename does not produce -- and the control never looked at it. Instances ten, eleven and twelve share one shape: **a message stating something the code did not measure**, sitting next to a number that contradicted it. The number was printed every time. What was missing every time was an assertion *on* it.<br><br>**Fixed, and verified red.** The control now keeps 40 lines of stable content so the rename is detectable, stages nothing, **asserts porcelain contains an `R` line with ` -> ` and a `??` line before scanning anything**, and **asserts the scan reports 0 skipped**. Defeating the parser fix (`if False:` on the destination branch) turns it red at 10 of 11, failing on the skipped-count assertion -- so the control now fails for the mechanism it names. The lesson generalises past this file: when a check prints a count beside a claim, the count is not decoration, and a control that does not assert on it is asserting on the claim alone.<br><br>**Thirteenth instance, appended by the m0c1 worker (M0-03).** `cli_exit_codes_distinguish_config_credentials_and_transport` in `crates/tunnel-client/src/main.rs` asserted that the CLI's exit-code table mapped `"CREDENTIAL_EXPIRED"` to `3` and `"TRANSPORT_ERROR"` to `4`. It was green for the life of the table and **could not have reddened for the defect that was actually present**: it built its own `CliError` from a code string it chose, and `CREDENTIAL_EXPIRED` is a *doctor* code, produced in `doctor.rs` against that module's own exit constants and never by any `ClientError`. The arm it exercised was dead. Meanwhile six live causes -- `OWNER_BUSY`, `CANCELLED`, `AUTHORIZATION_STALE`, `RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED`, `PROTOCOL_ERROR`, `SUPERVISOR_FAILED` -- had no entry at all and fell through `_ => 1`. **This one has no printed number**, which is where it differs from ten, eleven and twelve: the tell was not an unasserted figure but an unasserted *input*. The test chose the value whose handling it then verified, so the set of inputs it covered and the set the product produces were never compared, and nothing in the file named either set. The generalisation of the running tell: when a check constructs its own subject, ask what produces that subject in production -- if the answer is "nothing", the check is green over an empty domain. Fixed by driving every case from a constructed `ClientError` and by replacing the string table with a `Cause` enum whose `code`, `exit_code` and `from_client` matches are exhaustive, so an unclassified cause is a compile error rather than a silent `1`. Red-then-green evidence: `scripts/m0-guard-exit-codes.py`.<br><br>**Fourteenth instance, appended by the m6c2 worker (M6-01), and it is this worker's own code caught by the mechanism the previous instances asked for.** `scripts/m6-release-artifact.py`'s `assets` check declared two distinct witnesses for the sentinel -- `sentinel-missing` for an absent `tunnel-deadman` and `binary-missing` for an absent product command -- and `sentinel-missing` was **unreachable**: `tunnel-deadman` was also in the generic `BUNDLE_BINARIES` existence loop, which runs first, so deleting the sentinel produced `binary-missing` and the specific branch could never execute. The check was correct in outcome -- it went red -- and wrong in reason, which is exactly the distinction the running list keeps being about. **Nothing here printed a contradictory number; what caught it was the `--self-test` rule that a control must name the witness it expects**, imported from `scripts/m0-guard-exit-codes.py`'s `expected_red`. Had the control accepted any red, a dead code path would have shipped looking exercised, and the witness that distinguishes silent containment degradation from an unusable bundle -- two problems with different fixes -- would have been decorative. Fixed by removing `tunnel-deadman` from the generic loop and commenting why it is absent from it. **The wrong-witness mechanism was then itself shown red in both directions** rather than trusted because the suite was green: a control declaring a witness the check cannot produce is refused with `expected witness 'a-witness-that-cannot-fire', got 'sentinel-missing'`, and a control that declares the right witness but never defeats the mechanism is refused with `assets stayed GREEN with its mechanism defeated`.<br><br>**And the cheap tell fired once more in the same chunk, on prose.** A first draft of `docs/testing.md` said this script runs "thirteen controls". It ran **fourteen** at the time. The figure then had to be corrected to fifteen, to seventeen, and after the Fable review to **eighteen witness controls plus two unit probes** -- four corrections to one sentence, which is the argument for the script printing the figure rather than the prose carrying it, and for counting the two kinds separately rather than summing them. The number was written from memory of the list rather than measured from `CONTROLS`, which is the tell in its purest form -- a statement about a quantity the writer had not counted -- and it was caught by counting. The general form for a reviewer: **a figure in prose next to a script that can emit that figure is a figure that should have come from the script.**<br><br>**Fifteenth instance, appended by the m6c2 worker (M6-01) after the Fable review, and it is the most consequential form the shape has taken this session.** `scripts/m6-release-artifact.py`'s `notices` check was green against a `NOTICE` that contained **no licence texts** -- only each crate's SPDX identifier and the SHA-256 of its licence file. Every assertion around it was real and passed for real reasons: the crate set was re-derived from the bundled lockfile and matched exactly, the lockfile digest matched the header, 381 = 353 + 28 balanced in both directions, and a floor kept the crate count above 300. **None of them was the obligation.** MIT, the BSD family and Apache-2.0 require the copyright notice and the licence text to *accompany* a binary distribution; a digest lets a checker confirm nothing drifted and hands the recipient something they cannot read. So the check measured exactly the thing it named -- drift in a notice manifest -- and the thing it named was not the thing required, on the one row whose entire purpose is handing an artifact to an outside tester.<br><br>**This instance has no contradicting number at all**, which is where it differs from ten through twelve and from thirteen's unasserted input: nothing printed was false, the floor was not stale, and no input was self-chosen. The gap was between the check's subject and the deliverable's *purpose*, and no amount of internal consistency could surface it. The generalisation for a reviewer, and the reason it is worth recording separately: **when a check is named after an artifact, ask what the artifact is for, not only whether it is intact.** A manifest of hashes and a licence notice are both "notices" to a checker and only one of them discharges anything. Fixed by embedding all 628 licence files byte-exact (3,145,545 bytes) between delimiters, with the count and byte total recomputed from those delimiters rather than read off the header, and two new controls: stripping every text reddens on `embedded-text-count-mismatch`, and a NOTICE gutted to one text but edited to be *self-consistent* -- which defeats the count comparison -- reddens on `licence-text-floor`. **Found by the Fable review, not by this worker**, and not by seventeen controls that all passed.<br><br>**Sixteenth instance, appended by the m6c2 worker (M6-01) in the round that fixed instance fifteen, and it is the same defect one layer in.** The repaired `notices` check embedded 628 licence texts and reported them "**byte-exact**". It measured the number of blocks and their total byte count; it never compared a block to the digest recorded two lines above it. So the adjective was unearned in general -- filler of the same length would have passed both figures -- and **already false in particular**: `text.rstrip("\n")` had trimmed trailing newlines from 34 files, and reading the NOTICE back through `Path.read_text()` deleted carriage returns from two more. The Fable review caught the unearned adjective; binding the digests then caught the corruption, which no review had seen.<br><br>**The tell here is a new one and worth adding to the list: an adjective doing the work of an assertion.** "byte-exact", "complete", "verified" and "validated" are all claims a check either makes or does not, and this one sat in a message beside two numbers that were perfectly consistent with the corruption. The cheap question a reviewer can ask: *which line of code would fail if this adjective were false?* For "byte-exact" the answer was none. Fixed by embedding the text verbatim, carrying each file's SHA-256 in its own BEGIN marker, and re-hashing every reconstructed block at check time, with three controls -- same-length filler, a marker stripped of its digest, and a header that under-claims (the comparison was `<` rather than `!=`, so a header claiming *fewer* bytes than the body carried passed).<br><br>**And the instrument had the bug it was measuring.** The out-of-band verifier written to check byte-exactness against the registry reported 2 mismatches; the mismatches were in the verifier, which also used `read_text()`. Corrected, it reports 628 of 628 byte-identical. **When a measurement disagrees with the thing it measures, suspect the instrument before the artifact** -- both had to be read as bytes before either could be trusted.<br><br>**Instance eighteen, from `m4c36` (M4-33), and it is the *scope* tell rather than the adjective one.** The cell-count assertion M4-33 asked for did not exist, so nothing measured the table's shape at all; but the failure worth recording here is the one *inside the measurement that did happen*. The M6-04 re-count reported 13 rows carrying "an unescaped pipe" by counting pipes not preceded by a backslash. That predicate cannot distinguish a pipe inside a code span from a deliberate seventh column, and 11 of the 13 turned out to be the latter -- so the count was right, the diagnosis was wrong, and the prescribed fix ("one backslash per row") would have corrupted 11 rows had it been applied as written. **The tell: the measurement reported the *included* set and never characterised it.** Asking "what is each of these 13, individually?" costs one pass over the same lines and is what separated 2 from 11. **And the correction inherited the fault**, exactly as this row's fourth tell predicts: M4-33's title said three, the re-count said thirteen, and both described the same wrong species, because the second was computed with a refinement of the first instrument instead of from the mechanism. The fix re-derives from a parser that states its cell-boundary rule in source and proves it on the real header. **Also, one fail-open closed rather than noted:** `m7-evidence-guard.py`'s scan printed `PASS` when it matched zero rows, so the tables moving would have silenced every rule in it while the exit code stayed 0. It now exits 2, and `scripts/test_table_shape.py` holds a case that fails if it ever returns normally on an empty scan.<br><br>**Seventeenth instance, appended by the m6c3 worker (M6-C06), and it was in the first draft of the very check written to close that row.** `assert_client_sentinel_beside DIR CONTEXT` in `scripts/client-bundle-sentinel.sh` is the shared rule that a bundle containing `tunnel-client` contains a working `tunnel-deadman` beside it. Its first draft opened with `[ ! -e "$DIR/tunnel-client" ] && return 0`, on the perfectly sound reasoning that a directory holding no client is not this rule's business.
