Ten through twelve printed a figure nothing asserted on; thirteen chose its own input; sixteen used an adjective in place of an assertion. This one is **a deliberate, correct exemption whose boundary was not checked** -- "not applicable" and "verified" returned the same value and printed the same nothing. The reviewer's question that catches it is the standing one from `docs/testing.md` in its most literal form: *if this check were never called at all, what would be different in the output?* For the draft, nothing. The generalisation: **an early return for a case the rule does not cover is a second success path, and it needs to be as loud as the first.**<br><br>**Fixed three ways rather than one**, because any of them alone leaves a hole: a non-existent `DIR` is now fatal with witness `bundle-dir-missing`; the genuine no-client case says so out loud instead of returning quietly; and the success path prints the directory it verified and the probe exit it got, so a green line names what produced it. **The green control in `scripts/m6-guard-client-bundle-sentinel.py` requires that success line**, not merely a zero exit -- which is what makes the control a control, since a zero exit is exactly what a deleted call also produces. Red-then-green for the boundary itself is the case `the rule cannot be satisfied by being pointed at nothing`, which is red with witness `bundle-dir-missing`.<br><br>**Eighteenth instance, appended by the m6c3 worker, and it is the family seen from the other side: not a check that could not fail, but a _diagnosis_ that could not fail.** Running `scripts/m3-harness-verify.sh` four times at one tip gave two reds **in different gates with different signatures**, and both red logs carried `production membership pin publication failed closed … "membership runtime is not Ready"`. One warning present in two unrelated failures is a strong-looking common cause, and it was about to be written into a row as one. Counting the same warning in **every** run refuted it in a single command: **9 in red run 1, 2 in red run 3, and 10 in the green run 2 -- the most in the run that passed.**<br><br>**The tell is new to this list and cheaper than any of the others: the discriminating evidence was in the output nobody opens.** Ten through twelve were figures printed and never asserted on; thirteen was a self-chosen input; sixteen was an adjective standing in for an assertion; seventeen was an exemption whose boundary went unchecked. This one is none of those -- nothing printed was false and no boundary was crossed. **The proposed mechanism was simply never tested against the case that could refute it**, because the refuting case is a *passing* run, and logs of passing runs are not read. A hypothesis formed only from failure logs is fitted to one arm of the experiment and cannot come out false.<br><br>**The generalisation, which applies well beyond warnings**: before naming anything seen in a failure as its cause, count it in the successes. If it is there too, it is background. The green arm is the discriminator, and it is usually the arm that was thrown away. Recorded on M7-C88 as well, where it independently reproduces a conclusion that row's own control had already reached about a neighbouring warning -- which is itself the point, since two routes to the same answer is what distinguishes a measurement from a story.<br><br>**Instance nineteen, from `m6c4` (M6-C08), and it is the *adjective* tell landing on a product surface rather than on a test.** The tell is: take the word doing the claiming and ask which line fails if it is false. `doctor` reported `PROCESS_CONTAINMENT_SENTINEL_PRESENT`, and the answer was **no line at all** -- `resolve_sentinel` tested `is_file()`, so "present" meant "an entry of this name exists" while the reader takes it to mean "containment is present". A zero-byte 0644 decoy satisfied it. What makes this worth the entry rather than just being M6-C08's summary is **where** the tell applies: the previous eighteen instances are all checks, harnesses or prose, and this one is a *status code an operator reads*. The same question works there unchanged, and the vocabulary is where it has to be asked, because a status word is a claim with no assertion under it. The fix is recorded in the same place: `Armable`'s doc comment now states what it establishes and what it does not, and a test named `the_rule_cannot_tell_an_executable_impostor_from_the_real_sentinel` holds the limit so the adjective cannot drift back.<br><br>**Instance twenty, same chunk, and it is the fourth tell -- a correction applied to a bad instrument inheriting the fault -- caught before it was made rather than after.** The six new M6-C08 rules were going into `scripts/m3-guard-deletion.py`, which classified a case `RED` on **any** named failing test. Adding cases to it would have produced a tally that looked exactly like evidence and was not, which is `m0-guard-exit-codes.py`'s `expected_red` rationale arriving a second time by a different route. **Measured rather than argued, and re-measured after the Fable review changed the case list.** Of the seven cases in `m3c09-deadman`, the **execute-permission** case reddens **five** tests and the **present-vs-absent** case reddens **five**, overlapping in **four** -- so under "any red will do" either of those two rules could be credited by the other's witness, and defeating one while the other was already broken would still have printed a clean `7 of 7`. The contrast inside the same suite is the useful half: the **directory** case and the **`access`-versus-mode-bit** case redden **exactly one test each, their own**, which is what a case pinned to its rule looks like. A first draft of this sentence named the directory case as one of the overlapping pair; it is the opposite, and the review caught it -- **a narrative about a measurement is not the measurement**, which is this row's subject arriving one level up. So the mechanism was ported into that harness **first**, with its refusal (`require_declared_witnesses`) intact, and the six cases were added afterwards; the four pre-existing `m3c09` cases had their witnesses measured too rather than backfilled from whatever reddened. The general form: **when a chunk's evidence is about to be produced by an instrument weaker than the claim, fixing the instrument is part of the chunk, not a follow-up row** -- a follow-up leaves a tally standing that nobody will re-run.<br><br>**Instance twenty-one, same chunk, and it is the *reporting instrument* rather than any check: `$?` after a pipeline is the last command's status, so a whole chunk's worth of "EXIT=0" figures were `tail`'s and `grep`'s.** Written as `python3 scripts/m6-release-artifact.py verify --bundle DIR \| tail -20; echo "EXIT=$?"`, the reported code belongs to `tail`, which succeeds whatever the script did. Every such figure **would have read `0` for a red gate**, which is the defining shape of this row applied to the act of measuring: success and non-execution produce identical output. Two things made it visible rather than plausible. First a **real** miss -- a workspace tally read off a log that had been piped through `tail -40`, so it showed 7 of 148 test binaries and an exit code that was not cargo's, and the "pass" it produced was not evidence. Then the Fable review's note that **`${PIPESTATUS[0]}` is bash and expands empty under this repository's zsh** (`ZSH_VERSION=5.9`; the array is `$pipestatus[1]`, one-indexed) -- so the one place the pipeline's real status had been asked for printed nothing at all, and an empty figure was being read as a passing one. Every gate figure in M6-C08 was then re-measured as `cmd > log 2>&1; echo "EXIT=$?"`, which is the only form in this environment that reports the status of the thing being run. **The general rule, and it is cheap: never put a pager, `grep` or `tail` between a gate and the `$?` you are going to quote.** Inspect the log afterwards as a separate command.<br><br>**Instance twenty-two, and it is the sharpest form of the scope tell yet, because nothing could have caught it by defeating anything.** `crates/tunnel-relay/src/http.rs:2539-2545` states that "readiness and admission withdraw together and recover together, and no observer can see one without the other", citing the test `peer_readiness_and_admission_never_disagree` (`peer_runtime_probe_tests.rs:1136`). That test is **true, honest and empty**: `/readyz` is `health::ready_response(PeerRuntime::is_ready())` and public admission is `http::peer_admits_public_work`, which is **the same call**, as the test's own doc comment says ("They are one atomic read"). It samples **two views of one variable** and requires they never differ, which they cannot. The property the citing sentence reads as promising -- *readiness agrees with the thing it reports on* -- is not measured, and is **false**: neither view consults the verified pin set, so for up to one refresh tick both report ready while every peer dial is refused (M7-C89). **The excluded set is exactly where the disagreement lives.** **Why this shape outlives every other one in this row:** a check that cannot fail is caught the moment a guard case defeats it, because it stays green. This one goes *red* when defeated -- correctly, for the property it really measures -- so it survives every mutation a deletion harness can apply. The only thing that finds it is reading what the citing sentence claims against what the assertion covers.<br><br>**Instance twenty-three: a proposed measurement that is constant across both arms, so it confirms whatever hypothesis it is brought to.** M3-25 and M7-C83 asked future instances to record the **dispatch offset** of each failure, so that a cluster of offsets inside the pin-unavailable window would settle the race hypothesis by counting. The offset of the failing case is **20794 ms and 20771 ms in runs that passed** against **20695 ms** in one that failed and 20.6 s in the originally reported one -- a structural constant of the gate's case ordering, not a property of the failure. Every collected offset would have landed inside the window, so the pile would have grown at the same rate whether or not the hypothesis were true: **not a check that cannot fail, but a check that cannot come out the other way.** **The tell, and it is one command: take the statistic in the arm you are not interested in.** If a failure-only number is unchanged across the passes, it describes the shape of the population and not the defect.<br><br>**Instance twenty-four: an interval measured against its own endpoint, because a filtered log's first line was taken as t-zero.** Asked where in a run the `production membership pin publication failed closed` warnings fell, this worker subtracted the log's first timestamp from each warning's and reported "~5.85 s into the process, inside `ProductionCluster::start`". The harness defaults its tracing filter to `warn` and the gate sets no `RUST_LOG`, so **the log's first line *was* the first warning**: the origin and the measurement were the same event, and the plausible startup offset was the gap between two warnings. Re-derived from outside the filter -- file mtime minus the separately recorded elapsed seconds -- the same warnings are at **37.9 s of a 38 s run**, i.e. **teardown**, which is the opposite end and the opposite meaning. **The rule: never take a filtered log's first line as t-zero. Derive the origin from outside the filter, and say which origin you used**, because a wrong one produces a number with the right units and no way to notice.<br><br>**Instance twenty-five, and it is about the act of predicting rather than the act of checking: a prediction is pre-registered against a clock, not against one's own memory of not having looked.** While measuring M3-25 this worker wrote a falsifiable prediction into `docs/tasks.md` describing it as recorded "before the campaign that could refute it finished". **File times say otherwise:** the falsifying run's log was written at 21:56:14 and `docs/tasks.md` at 21:56:21 -- seven seconds later. The worker genuinely had not read the run, and **that is not the test**: the claim in the row was about the order of events, nothing in the repository could ever have checked it, and the incentive ran entirely one way. The edit was reverted and the claim removed rather than left standing with a caveat. **The general form: any claim of the shape "I did X before knowing Y" must be settled against a timestamp neither you nor the reader has to trust**, and if no such timestamp exists the claim should not be made at all -- an unverifiable priority claim in a durable row is strictly worse than no claim, because it reads as evidence and cannot be audited.<br><br>**Instance twenty-six, and the reason to record it is that the author had written instance twenty-two the same day.** Building the forced-window arm for M3-25, this worker wrote a test named `the_same_window_is_not_waited_for_when_the_rule_is_defeated` which defined a closure returning `false`, asserted that it returned `false`, asserted the real rule returned `true`, and **never ran the wait at all**. True, honest, and measuring something adjacent to its own name -- instance twenty-two's exact shape, reproduced hours after that instance was filed, by the person who filed it. It would have passed no matter what the loop did. **The lesson is not that the shape can be learned away but that it cannot be**: it is caught only by asking, of each test, which line of production code could change and leave it green. Its replacement runs the real loop and asserts one state with two outcomes.<br><br>**Instance twenty-seven: a test that FAILED and was right to, because its premise was wrong rather than the code.** The replacement above first asserted that an `installed_before` of `false` releases a relay from the wait. It went red. The rule holds a relay outstanding when a publication is still pending **or** when a set that was installed is now empty, and the **first clause is independent of `installed_before`** -- a publication that failed closed is outstanding whoever it belongs to. **Had that test passed it would have been asserting the rule was weaker than it is**, and it would have been kept as evidence that it was. Recorded because the reflex on a red test is to change the code, and here the code was right; the cheap discriminator is to ask what the test would have proved had it passed.<br><br>**Instance twenty-eight: a guard that witnessed a rule's decision and not its application, on the branch that catalogued instances twenty-two to twenty-seven.** `m3c25-resign-pin-wait` defeated `pin_publication_outstanding` three ways and reported three of three, each on its own declared witness -- everything instance twenty asks for. The Fable review of `3cf2c1e` then deleted the one line that *called* the wait, and separately made its bound proceed instead of failing, and the suite still said three of three. Every witness exercised the decision function, or the wait loop, directly; none could see whether the rule was ever **applied**. The suite's own comment named this exact shape as the one it existed to refuse. **The tell: for each rule, find the line that applies it and ask which case deletes that line.** A suite whose every case edits the predicate and never the call is measuring whether the rule is correct, not whether it runs. Here the application sat in code no unit test could reach -- a function that needs a Redis-backed cluster -- which is why no case could have been written against it, and why the fix was to move the application into reachable code rather than to add a case. Recorded against this worker because the author of instances twenty-two to twenty-seven wrote it, and because a per-case witness standard, met perfectly, did not catch it: **declared witnesses guarantee each case is attributed correctly, not that the set of cases covers the rule.** **Instance twenty-nine: a check whose scope was narrower than four documents said it was, found by review of the branch that built it (M6-02).** `scripts/m6-release-artifact.py`'s `docs` check was described in operator.md, the script's docstring, testing.md and the M6-02 row as failing on any shell block that was neither executed nor shape-only. Its classifier looked only at the tags it expected and `continue`d past everything else, so a mistyped `consol`, an untagged fence, a transcript retagged as prose and whole deleted sections all left it green, with a floor of 20 against 35 measured as the only guard, and nothing asserting on the counts it printed. Its controls were all green because every one of them planted a mutation *the classifier already recognised*. **The tell: for every rule a check claims to enforce, name the input the check would *skip*, and require that input to be a red.** An allowlist that refuses the unrecognised, plus pinned counts instead of a floor, closes the class; the controls now include the five inputs the review showed skipped. Upstream is explicit that **positive is up** in three places -- macOS (`y: Vertical scroll amount (positive for up, negative for down)`), Windows (`Positive values scroll up`) and the VNC connection (`y>0 = up, y<0 = down (matches macOS native handler convention)`) -- while Linux's docstring says only `The vertical scroll amount` and Android's inverts it explicitly for swipe (`end_y = center_y - y`). The point is therefore **still enforced and never transmitted**: it gates whether the scroll is allowed, and does not decide where it lands. Upstream scrolls wherever the cursor happens to be.<br><br>**That is not obviously the wrong behaviour, which is why it is a row rather than a fix.** Keeping the bounds check means a consumer cannot use `scroll` to reach outside the image it looked at, which is the confinement the capture identity exists for, and it costs nothing. But a consumer reasonably reads `scroll(capture, point, dy)` as "scroll at this point", and it is not. The candidate fixes differ in kind: **compose** it -- `move_cursor` to the point under the same lease, then `scroll` -- which makes the promise true at the cost of a second command and a visible cursor move that the consumer did not ask for and that cannot be undone if the scroll then fails; or **narrow the schema** so `scroll` takes no point and says so, which is honest and removes the confinement check with it. Narrowing avoids that window entirely -- `Params::Scroll` is `{dx, dy}`, `scroll` no longer needs a capture identity (it still needs the lease), and a request naming `capture`, `x` or `y` is refused with `SchemaError::UnknownMember` rather than validated and dropped. A consumer that wants a position sends `move` (validated against its capture) and then `scroll`, and gets an explicit outcome for each step, so the composition the row wanted exists with each half's outcome reported rather than hidden. The confinement the old bounds check appeared to give was never real: the point was not transmitted. **The sign is now pinned** as `cua_pin::SCROLL_SIGN_CONVENTION` -- positive `dy` is up, quoting the pinned macOS, Windows and VNC handlers, with Linux (unstated) and Android (swipe mapping) recorded as inferred -- and `tests/cua_pin.rs` requires `integrations.md` to tell consumers so. **Red first:** `plan::tests::a_scroll_that_names_a_position_is_refused_rather_than_silently_not_honoured` (nonce `411e1e6c174b`: left `Ok(Planned::Dispatch { command: "scroll", ... })`). The reap status was `SIGKILL`, and the test's observation was `row=Z, killed=1, group_kills=0, exited=0`. `group_kills` reached 1 within 0-2 ms of polling in every case. No run took the natural-exit branch for this test's pid. The sentinel cannot be the killer: it fires only when its stdin reaches EOF without the stand-down byte, which needs this process to die. In the sentinel-absent half, nothing was armed at all. `kill_on_drop` cannot be the killer either, because the supervisor task owns the tokio `Child` until after the reap.<br><br>**Fix, test-only, and no weaker than before.** Before the drop, the test clones the handle's `exited` receiver. ## M6 — operable private alpha and release artifacts

| ID | Task | Status | Owner | Acceptance or evidence | Completed at |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| M6-01 | [ ] Produce clean-machine binaries for every advertised OS/architecture with checksums, provenance, notices, and required runtime assets. | in progress (1 of 4 targets passes the maintainer gate; all 4 are built, smoke-tested and published by hosted CI without it -- M6-C13 owner decision) | release | **One release bundle for `aarch64-apple-darwin` is produced and its six gate checks pass against the unpacked artifact. The row is not closed, and the reason is not "the other platforms are pending" -- it is that nothing in this repository declares what the platforms are.**<br><br>**Step-1 measurement, before building anything.** The row's criterion turns on the word *advertised*, and **the word has no referent**. Grepping every `.md`, `.toml` and `.yml` outside `vendor/` for target triples returns prose only; root `Cargo.toml` carries no platform metadata; `packages/client/package.json` is `private: true` with no `os`/`cpu`; `README.md` names "macOS arm64" once, as the machine the M1 evidence was taken on. The nearest thing is `.github/workflows/ci.yml`'s `os: [ubuntu-latest, macos-latest, windows-latest]` -- three runner *labels*, no architecture -- which `testing.md` disqualifies in the same paragraph that asks the question ("macOS/Linux/Windows CI success is not by itself evidence for every architecture"). `deny.toml` reasons about "the advertised release targets" as though the set existed. **So the criterion's completeness clause is unsatisfiable by anyone but the owner, and any claim to have built for "every" target would be a claim about a set the claimant chose.** Filed as M6-C04 with the measurements.<br><br>**What the gate actually asks for, read as the specification rather than the row's summary.** `testing.md` wants checksums, provenance, notices, required runtime assets, help/version/config checks **from the unpacked artifact**, no workspace-only dependency masking a missing file, and -- separately -- a launched relay and device doing a real consumer-to-device operation and a rotation. **The last clause is not covered by this chunk and is not claimed**; what is covered is the artifact's integrity, provenance, notices, assets and CLI surface. Before this chunk none of it existed: there was no bundle, no notices file of any kind (`NOTICE` did not exist; only the workspace's own `LICENSE`), and no check that ran a binary from anywhere but `target/`.<br><br>**What this host can produce, measured in both directions rather than assumed, because "cross-compilation is available" and "an artifact is producible" are different claims.** `rustup target list --installed` showed three targets; each was probed by building the workspace's smallest binary. `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` **compiles and cannot link** -- Apple's `ld` rejects the GNU options rustc passes (`ld: unknown options: --as-needed -Bstatic -Bdynamic --eh-frame-hdr -z --gc-sections -z -z --strip-debug`), which is precisely the case where a cross-target `cargo check` is green and there is no artifact. `x86_64-pc-windows-msvc` **compiles and cannot link** -- `linker 'link.exe' not found`. `x86_64-apple-darwin` was *not* installed; adding it **linked successfully**, producing a real `Mach-O 64-bit executable x86_64` -- and it **cannot be executed here**, because Rosetta 2 is absent (`bad CPU type in executable`; `/usr/bin/arch -x86_64 /usr/bin/true` fails the same way). The gate requires the checks to run *from the unpacked artifact*, so that triple is producible and unverifiable, and shipping it either way would misrepresent it. MIT, the BSD family and Apache-2.0 require the copyright notice and the licence text to *accompany* a binary distribution; a digest lets a checker confirm nothing drifted and gives the recipient nothing they can read. | M6-C16 | [x] Every agent in a session shares one scratchpad directory, so a generic log filename silently resolves to another worker's stale output and reads exactly like a fresh result. | verified local | tooling/process; fixed by the m6-release worker | **Caught in the act, one step before a wrong figure went into this tracker.** A release bundle was rebuilt and its result read back from `<scratchpad>/bundle2.log`. The log said the bundle was written to `/private/tmp/m6c4-bundle2` with archive sha256 `10b6eccbecfe...`. **Neither was this worker's.** The `--out` passed was `<scratchpad>/rel2`, and `/private/tmp/m6c4-bundle2` is a path this worker never named. The file was dated **21:12**; the run reading it started at **23:50**. It was a **pre-existing file from the `m6c4` worker**, and this worker's own bundle step was still running and had not yet truncated it.<br><br>**The mechanism.** The per-session scratchpad is keyed on the *session*, not the agent, and this session has run dozens of agents concurrently (`m6c1`..`m6c5`, `m4c3x`, `m5c5`..`m5c8`, and more). They all write into the same directory. **185 `.log` files were already there.** Obvious names -- `bundle.log`, `parity.log`, `verify.log`, `chain-test.log` -- are exactly the ones several workers pick independently, so a collision is likely rather than exotic.<br><br>**Why this is a measurement defect and not a housekeeping annoyance.** A stale log is byte-for-byte indistinguishable from a fresh one: it has plausible content, in the right format, at the right path. `cmd > log 2>&1; echo $?` does not protect against it either, because the exit code read is the *current* command's while the content read can be the *previous occupant's* if the command has not yet written -- which is precisely what happened here, with a backgrounded step still running. This is the M5-C11 shape in the *instrument's storage* rather than in its logic: an output that looks like it ran and did not. It sits beside the falsification control recorded in M6-04 -- whose fixture loader failed to import, so nothing was ever planted and the scan honestly reported 0 on an unchanged repository -- as the second instance in this chunk of the measuring apparatus, not the subject, being wrong.<br><br>**What saved it, and it was not discipline.** The log printed a `--out` path that did not match the one passed. **The tell was a value the reader could cross-check against something they already knew**, and the general lesson is that a result should carry enough identity to be attributable -- which is the same argument `PROVENANCE.txt` makes for binaries, applied to log files. **Scope of the contamination, checked rather than assumed**: every other log this chunk read was timestamped inside its own working window (23:11-23:51), and the first bundle's `PROVENANCE.txt` independently names this branch's commit `0ef7c31`, so **no figure reported by this chunk came from another worker**. when one ends by itself, `Cause::reconnect_class` -- an exhaustive match with **no fallback arm**, like `Cause::exit_code` -- decides. **Terminal:** `INVALID_INVOCATION`/`CONFIG_ERROR`/`INVALID_CONFIG` (local input; the profile is read once), `CREDENTIAL_ERROR` (local credential unreadable, or a TLS certificate refusal, below), `CANCELLED`, `PROTOCOL_ERROR` (version skew or a violation; TLS rules out corruption), `SUPERVISOR_FAILED`, `SIGNAL_ERROR`. **Retryable:** `TRANSPORT_ERROR`, `SESSION_CLOSED`, `DEADLINE_EXCEEDED`, `RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED` (a per-session budget; the library says start a fresh session) and `AUTHORIZATION_STALE` (its only producer is a per-stream operation deadline lapsing with a frame queued, not a revocation -- filed as M6-C39 because exit `3`'s advice is wrong for it). **Conditional:** `OWNER_BUSY` is retried only within 60 s of this process's own ready session ending -- the relay's stale owner lease -- and is terminal on a fresh process's first attempt, so a second connector still exits `7` at once -- witnessed only by the unit test `owner_busy_is_retried_only_within_the_window_after_our_own_session`, because the M7 ownership gates spawn the binary with `--no-reconnect` and never reach the loop (corrected on review). The justification of every arm is in runtime.md ("Reconnecting `connect`"), pinned by `reconnect_classification_matches_the_documented_table`. **The TLS line, classified by rustls variant before sanitization** (`tls_refusal`, `lib.rs`), narrowed twice on coordinator review: terminal `ClientError::TlsRefused` (`CREDENTIAL_ERROR`, exit `3`, a fixed reason, nothing from the peer) for an unknown issuer, bad signature, revoked, wrong name or wrong purpose on the relay's certificate and for an unknown-CA, bad, unsupported, revoked, unknown or required certificate alert from the relay; **retryable with its reason** for validity **time** -- the relay's certificate expired or not yet valid on this host's clock, and the relay's `certificate_expired` alert, which rustls 0.23 sends for an expired **and** a not-yet-valid client certificate alike (`impl From<CertificateError> for AlertDescription`, checked in the pinned source), judged on the relay's clock: `connect` then reads **its own certificate against its own clock** (`attempt_error`, `main.rs`, `doctor`'s chain-wide window) and exits `3` naming the expiry only when it is past `notAfter` here too, otherwise retries with a message naming clock skew; opaque and retryable for everything else (reset, EOF, I/O, timeout, `handshake_failure`, `decrypt_error`, `access_denied`, unlisted certificate errors). **Backoff:** the n-th consecutive retry waits uniform in `[c/2, c]`, `c = min(initial * 2^(n-1), max)`; defaults 1 s, 60 s cap, no attempt limit; validation 100 ms to 300 s. The floor stops a busy loop against a relay that refuses at once, the half-ceiling spread separates devices that lost one relay together (jitter from the OS generator via `uuid` v4), the cap bounds a device's absence after its relay is back, and the count resets only after a session stayed ready for `max_delay_ms`, so a relay that accepts and drops still backs off. `[reconnect] enabled / initial_delay_ms / max_delay_ms / max_attempts` in the profile, and `--no-reconnect` for one run. **A stop during the backoff exits `130` `CANCELLED` at once** (`SIGTERM received while waiting to reconnect (attempt N, after CODE); no session was live`): not `0`, because `0` means a completed orderly stop of a live session and no session is live; the same rule as a stop before the first session was ready, and the same status a stop 1 ms later, in the next attempt's handshake, gives; systemd units list `SuccessExitStatus=130`. **Events** under `--json`: `disconnected`, `backoff`, `reconnecting`, `reconnected`, with attempt and session counters, session id, `ready_ms`, `delay_ms` and the cause's code and bounded message; no payloads. The `ready`/`stopped` events' `failure_policy` no longer claims "no automatic reconnect" while the loop is on. **Children:** the handler registry is built per attempt and dropped with the connector, so supervised MCP and ACP children are **restarted, not kept** -- a child never outlives the device session its requests came in on (M3-04), and its protocol session could not be resumed through a new relay session anyway; the loop waits (bounded, 5 s) for MCP reaps before backing off (M6-C28's residual gap unchanged). Rotation state belongs to the session and starts afresh; a reconnect is a new session id, epoch and generation. **Harness spawns that assert first-session-end behaviour** (`start_cli_smoke`, `ownership::spawn_cli`, `i08_synthetic_rotation`) and `a_refused_relay_connection_exits_four_and_names_the_transport` now pass `--no-reconnect`; an audit of every real-binary spawn found no other dependency. **Integration with M6-C32 (PR #91):** a single relay now closes an identity refusal `1008` `DEVICE_IDENTITY_REJECTED`, which the client reports `CREDENTIAL_ERROR`, so the loop exits `3` after one attempt -- measured on the merged tip (`m6c23_an_identity_mismatch_exits_three_without_retrying`); every new `CredentialError` variant #91 added reaches the loop as `Cause::CredentialError` through `ClientError::Credential(_)` and is terminal, which is right because each is a local certificate/key/profile fault or the relay's identity refusal; M6-C32's own identity cases now run with reconnect on and assert no `backoff`, and its not-yet-valid case (a catalog `not_before` ahead, a bare close, retryable) passes `--no-reconnect`. **Discovered and filed:** M6-C38 (the HELLO refusals still given without a reason -- protocol major, and the cluster path M6-C43 -- arrive as retryable `TRANSPORT_ERROR` and are retried, visibly and bounded only by `max_attempts`), M6-C39 (`AUTHORIZATION_STALE`'s exit-3 advice), M6-C40 (a SIGKILLed relay's owner records refuse its devices for about 30 s), M6-C41 (an intermittent `verify-m2-faults` red, reproduced on `origin/main` at the same rate).<br><br>**Tests, each red for its own reason.** `crates/tunnel-client/tests/reconnect_cli.rs` (13, ordinary workspace suite, local stand-ins using the same rustls verifier as the relay): bounded jittered delays and the attempt limit; Green on m6-ops in `m6-provisioning-verify.sh` (`m6c24-metrics ok`, nonce `m6ops-chain-m6prov-20260925T100415Z-77038`); C11 twice and `verify-m7-i04-fail-closed` on the tip (history row). operator.md section 5 and runtime.md updated. **Mixed versions:** an older relay refuses a configuration naming `metrics_bind` (unknown field); remove it before rolling back. **Still open, why this row stays open:** (1) the owner decision on which metrics and audit events the alpha needs, which this row's acceptance names first -- the delivered set is the worker's choice from runtime.md's contract, not a decision; (2) metrics runtime.md lists and this does not measure: rotation duration and overlap, credit stalls, peer RTT, request latency, device TLS and session refusals; (3) no authentication on the listener, only its address; (4) **no audit log**. An audit log needs: the owner's event set (catalog changes, grant/device/credential revocations, `rebind-redis-run`, recovery approvals, refused privileged operations); an append-only, bounded-retention Redis stream under its own namespace keys (no second store), written in the **same Lua script** as the change it records so a change without its record cannot commit; an actor/tenant/target/outcome schema with identifiers only; an authenticated read surface; and redaction tests that can fail.<br><br>**PR #158 review follow-up (`1b4986f`).** The listener is `metrics::serve_bounded`, not `axum::serve`: at most 4 connections (one more is closed at accept), hyper's 2 s request-head deadline, no keep-alive, and a 10 s lifetime per connection; it stops at cancel. | M6-C40 | [ ] After a relay dies without releasing its owner records (SIGKILL, crash, host loss), its devices are refused `OWNER_BUSY` -- by the restarted relay too -- until the owner lease lapses, about 30 s with the default `owner_lease`. | discovered defect (measured; decision needed: options and a recommendation recorded) | relay (found by the m6c23 reconnect worker) | **Measured on the real binaries** (`m6c23_connect_reconnects_after_the_relay_is_killed_and_after_it_is_stopped`, four runs, the last on the merged tip `55de8b1`, log nonce `m6c23r-reconnect-20260923T083210Z-2522`): after `serve` was SIGKILLed mid-session and restarted with the same configuration (same `node_id` and `boot_id`), the client's reconnects were refused `OWNER_BUSY` (38 to 40 times under the gate's short policy; about five under the defaults, derived) and it reconnected 29.8--30.4 s after the new relay was listening; after an orderly SIGTERM stop, which releases the owner, in 499--866 ms. **Mechanism, by source:** `SCRIPT_CLAIM_OWNER_BODY` (`crates/tunnel-catalog/src/redis.rs`) answers `busy` while the record's `lease_expires_at_us` is in the future unless deployment incarnation, node, boot **and session** id all match, and a new relay process has a new session id; `owner_lease` is bounded 6..=30 s (`crates/tunnel-relay/src/config.rs`). `connect` now rides it out -- `OWNER_BUSY` is retried for 60 s after its own session ended -- so the device recovers, but every relay crash is a ~30 s outage for its devices, and a relay that stays dead does not shorten it. Documented in operator.md sections 3.1 and 4 ("stop relays with SIGTERM, not SIGKILL"). **Acceptance:** an owner decision: accept and keep the documentation; lower `owner_lease` for single-relay deployments; or let a relay reclaim records of a provably dead earlier process of the same node, which needs a fencing argument against M7-C02's incarnation-scoped leases.<br><br>**m6-ops (2026-09-25): options and a recommendation, decision still needed; nothing changed in code.** Re-read at `f9f7abf`: `SCRIPT_CLAIM_OWNER_BODY` answers `busy` while `lease_expires_at_us` is ahead unless incarnation, node, boot **and** session all match, and cluster.md defines `boot_id` as the identifier that "prevents a restarted process claiming its predecessor's live state" -- so the ~30 s wait is that rule working, and any shortening has to prove the predecessor dead rather than assume it. **(a) Accept and keep the documentation** (operator.md 3.1 and 4: stop with SIGTERM, which releases). Cost: every crash, OOM kill or host loss is an outage of up to `owner_lease` (30 s default) for that relay's devices; `connect` already rides it out. **(b) Lower `owner_lease` for single-relay deployments** (bounded 6..=30 s today). Cost: renewals every `owner_lease/3`, so a 9 s lease renews every 3 s and loses ownership after a Redis stall of about 6 s -- close to the 2 s operation deadline plus the M6-C74 10 s reconnect budget -- trading a crash outage for spurious session loss during Redis blips; it shortens the outage, it does not remove it. **(c) Reclaim on proof of death: a node boot fence.** At startup the relay atomically replaces `coord:node:<incarnation>:<node_id>` with its own `boot_id` (TTL'd like presence); `claim_owner` may take a live record whose node equals the claimant's and whose `boot_id` differs from the fence, and `renew_owner`/`release_owner` refuse a record whose `boot_id` is not the fence's -- all in the same Lua scripts, so the old process is fenced in the same step that the new one reclaims. Fencing argument: the only process that can write the fence for a node is one holding that node's configuration; after the swap the predecessor can no longer renew, so the reclaim cannot create two owners. Risks, stated: two live processes misconfigured with the same `node_id` would now steal each other's devices instead of one being refused `OWNER_BUSY` (the fence makes that visible as ownership flapping, and a cluster relay's node identity is already bound to its signed membership key); records written by pre-fence relays carry no fence and must stay non-reclaimable, so mixed versions degrade to (a); the fence is incarnation-scoped, so M7-C02's incarnation-scoped leases are untouched. **Recommendation: (c)**, because it removes the outage for the common restart-in-place case (same `node_id`, which a systemd unit or Fly machine keeps) without weakening the lease against Redis stalls, keeping (a)'s documentation until it lands; not (b), which moves the outage onto Redis blips. The implementation needs the three scripts, a real-Redis test that SIGKILLs a relay and restarts it with the same `node_id` and reconnects well under the lease, and a two-process test that the fenced predecessor's renewal is refused. **Owner decision needed:** (a), (b) or (c), and whether same-`node_id` stealing is acceptable. | — |

| M6-C68 | [ ] A relay whose device's network path vanished keeps the old session forever: it sends no pings, reads the control socket without a timeout, sets no `SO_KEEPALIVE`, keeps renewing the owner lease, and refuses every reconnect of that device `OWNER_BUSY` until the relay is restarted. | implemented awaiting verification | relay (found by the M6-C23 review of `dbea3a4`; filed by the m6c23 reconnect worker; implemented by the m6-c68-liveness worker) | **Measured by the reviewer on `dbea3a4`, not re-run by this worker:** a TCP proxy cut the client's side of the control and data sockets while holding the relay's side open and idle -- what a laptop waking on a new network, a NAT rebinding or a VPN drop looks like. `tunnel-client connect` (reconnect on) saw `control read failed` at 0 ms, then **78 `OWNER_BUSY` refusals and exit `7` at 60.7 s**, when `OWNER_BUSY_RECONNECT_WINDOW` ran out; the relay was alive and still held the old session (`relay_sockets_held=2`); no second `ready`. **Mechanism, by source (reviewer's reading, cited):** `register_control` answers `OwnerBusy` for any scope still in `self.sessions` before consulting the catalog (`crates/tunnel-relay/src/actor.rs`, about line 3436); `handle_control`'s loop (`crates/tunnel-relay/src/http.rs`, about 3841--3862) has no read timeout; nothing in `crates/tunnel-relay/src` constructs a `Ping`; no socket in the relay, transport or client sets `SO_KEEPALIVE`; the stale session renews its lease every `owner_lease/3` (`actor.rs`, about 12339). **Consequences:** the device cannot come back until the relay restarts; a supervisor's restart does not help, because a fresh process's first-attempt `OWNER_BUSY` is terminal by design (M6-C23), so under the original example unit's start limit the unit ended **failed** about 210 s after the network event -- changed on the M6-C23 branch to no start limit, so it retries every 30 s visibly and recovers once the relay lets go; launchd retries every 30 s. Documented in runtime.md ("Reconnecting `connect`") and operator.md sections 3.1 and 4. **Acceptance:** a relay-side fix -- replace the session on a re-HELLO authenticated by the same device key (with a fencing argument against M7-C02's incarnation-scoped leases), or liveness detection (control pings with a read deadline, or keepalive) that ends a dead session within a stated bound -- plus a real-binary test that reproduces the reviewer's cut-path proxy and requires a second `ready` within that bound. Not fixed on the M6-C23 branch by instruction.<br><br>**Implemented at `97ebf9c` (branch `m6-c68-liveness`, based on `721ed2a`): liveness eviction, not replacement on re-HELLO.** The owner-local control task (`handle_control`, `crates/tunnel-relay/src/http.rs`) sends a WebSocket Ping every `DEVICE_CONTROL_PING_INTERVAL` (10 s) and ends the session once no inbound frame of any kind -- text, Ping, or the Pong owed to its Ping -- has arrived for `DEVICE_CONTROL_IDLE_TIMEOUT` (30 s). Only inbound frames move the deadline (`ControlLiveness`): a relay write completes into the kernel's buffer on a dead path and proves nothing. The exit is the ordinary `finish_control_task` hand-off a device's own close takes (`disconnect_control` then `close_session`), so the session, its data carrier and its owner slot are released exactly as on a clean close; the closure is recorded under a new bounded cause, `liveness_timeout` (added to `TaskClosureCause` and to the C11 scanner's closed vocabulary), and logged with `phase="control_liveness_timeout"`, identifiers only. Both constants live in `tunnel-protocol` (`control.rs`) with compile-time bounds beside them: interval 1..=15 s, idle timeout at most 30 s and at least three intervals (a live device must miss two consecutive Pongs to be evicted). `tunnel-client` asserts at compile time that its `OWNER_BUSY_RECONNECT_WINDOW` (60 s) is at least the idle timeout plus the relay's 5 s disconnect hand-off plus 15 s. **Stated bound:** a relay ends a vanished device's session at most 30 s after the device's last frame, plus the bounded 5 s disconnect hand-off; the device is readmitted at its first attempt after that. Documented in operator.md section 3.1 (and section 4, whose client-unit rationale now names what the unit still covers) and runtime.md.<br><br>**Why eviction rather than replacing the session on a fresh HELLO from the same key.** (1) A second authenticated HELLO for the same key is not evidence that the first session is dead: a copied profile or a second `connect` holds the same certificate, and replacement would let the two steal the device from each other in turn. FP-08, EC-004 and IN-08 (docs/m7-edge-cases.md) require the opposite -- a duplicate exact-scope claim is terminal and the active owner stays authoritative -- and the first-attempt `OWNER_BUSY` rule M6-C23 relies on is built on that. (2) Replacement is a new ownership transition: it needs the fencing argument against M7-C02's incarnation-scoped leases this row's acceptance names, and on a cluster the new HELLO can land on a relay that does not own the session, so it would need a remote eviction path. Eviction adds no transition: it is the path a device's own close already takes, with the epoch, `STREAM_FORGET` state and owner record handled as they are today, and a healthy session is never evicted while it answers Pings. (3) M6-C40 is unaffected and still a design question: it concerns a relay process that died, which no liveness check in that process can shorten. **The cost:** up to about 30 s of `OWNER_BUSY` after a path change, measured below, inside the client's 60 s window.<br><br>**A correction to the relayed mechanism, re-derived from the source at `721ed2a`.** The reviewer's reading holds (no Ping constructed anywhere in `tunnel-relay/src`; the control loop has no read deadline). One more fact matters to the fix: the control loop had **no `Pong` arm**, so an inbound WebSocket Pong fell into `_ => UnexpectedMessage` and closed the session. Adding Pings without that arm would have evicted every healthy device at its first Pong; the fix adds the arm, and the healthy-idle half of the test below is red without it. `SO_KEEPALIVE` was not added: kernel defaults (2 h on macOS and Linux) are far outside any useful bound, and the WebSocket Ping crosses Fly's TCP passthrough unchanged.<br><br>**Tests, each confirmed red with its part of the fix removed.** (a) Real binaries, the reviewer's cut path: `m6c68_a_relay_evicts_a_device_whose_path_vanished_and_admits_its_reconnect` (`crates/tunnel-relay/tests/m6_reconnect_process.rs`, run by `scripts/m6-reconnect-verify.sh`, which now requires 7 passed and the `m6c68-liveness ok label=cut-path` line). The client reaches the relay through a TCP proxy. A healthy session is left idle for 40 s (idle timeout plus one interval) and must show no `disconnected` or `backoff` event and still echo; then the proxy drops the client's half of every connection and holds the relay's half open and silent (at least 2 held), the client must see `lost`, at least one `OWNER_BUSY` backoff (so the relay really did hold the dead session), and a second `ready` with a new session id within `CUT_PATH_RECONNECT_BOUND` = 40 s (itself asserted under 60 s), then an echo. **Green:** reconnect 30257 ms after the cut, 40 `OWNER_BUSY` refusals (single run on the uncommitted fix over `721ed2a`, log nonce `c68-20260923T130631Z-52288`); 30105 ms, 39 refusals in the full gate at `97ebf9c` (log nonce `c68-20260923T131919Z-61873`, gate `7 passed`). **Red, each measured with the relay rebuilt:** relay source restored to `721ed2a` -- the client got no `reconnected` within 40 s (`step reconnect after the cut: fewer than 1 reconnected events within 40s`, log nonce `c68-20260923T130823Z-54380`, exit 101, 81.8 s); the Pong arm alone removed -- `a healthy idle session must survive 40s` (nonce `c68-20260923T131009Z-55183`, exit 101, 41.6 s); the deadline never reset by inbound frames -- the same assertion (nonce `c68-20260923T131113Z-55455`, exit 101, 41.5 s). (b) Unit: `http::tests::control_liveness_deadline_follows_only_the_latest_inbound_frame`, red (exit 101) when `observe_inbound` may move the deadline backwards (nonce `c68-20260923T131210Z-56154`). The red runs were on the working tree over `721ed2a` before the commit, with only the named part of `http.rs` mutated. Not covered by a test: the WriteFailed exit of a failed Ping write (the same bounded 5 s `send_socket` as every other write).<br><br>**Not covered, and not claimed.** (1) **A device attached through a non-owner cluster relay.** `handle_remote_device_control` forwards the device socket to the owner over the peer stream and has no Ping or deadline, so on a cluster the ingress relay can still hold a vanished device's peer stream open and the owner keeps the session. The single-relay Fly deployment does not take this path. It needs the same liveness in that loop and a multi-relay cut-path test; left open in this row. (2) The client's own detection of a path that dies silently in both directions (no FIN or RST reaching it) was not measured; the reviewer's cut, reproduced here, reaches the client at once. (3) A relay older than `97ebf9c` still holds the session; the client unit's no-start-limit setting keeps that visible and self-healing (operator.md section 4).<br><br>**Checks at `97ebf9c`, each run separately; the tip adds docs only.** `cargo test --workspace --locked` exit 0: 155 `test result:` lines, 2211 passed, 0 failed (log nonce `c68-20260923T131443Z-57338`). `scripts/m6-reconnect-verify.sh` exit 0 (above). `scripts/m2-harness-verify.sh` exit 0 (nonce `c68-20260923T132145Z-62583`). `scripts/m6-provisioning-verify.sh` exit 0 (nonce `c68-20260923T132344Z-63449`). `scripts/m7-harness-verify.sh` exit 0, `implemented M7 harness suite passed` (nonce `c68-20260923T132450Z-66061`). The harness's raw test devices therefore survived the new Pings. Each of those logs records `head=97ebf9c` with `dirty_tracked_files=3`, which were docs/operator.md, docs/runtime.md and the client service example's comment, not code. **Remaining for `verified`:** an independent review, and item (1) above (the non-owner cluster ingress path), whether as scope for this row or as a new row.<br><br>**Review follow-up at `13e2299` (Opus approved `4a59158` with no must-fixes; `origin/main` at `946bcde` merged cleanly as `58b5347`).** (1) The control loop's `select!` is now `biased`, with the inbound arm first and the idle deadline last. | M6-C65 | [x] Every Redis restart makes `serve` refuse its namespace for good, even with persistence and every key intact, and nothing shipped recovers it. | verified (local and hosted) | m6-c65-redis-restart worker (found and measured by the m6-dogfood-local worker) | **Found** (unchanged): **Measured** (dogfood run; release bundle built from `496396e`, the tester's own CA, Redis 8.4.0 in Docker with an ACL user, password, TLS and client certificates, one relay without `[cluster]`, provisioned only with the shipped commands; log nonces `dogfood-redis-restart-20260923T095019Z-89307` and `dogfood-redis-restart-clean-20260923T095142Z-90674`). Clean case: a new namespace was provisioned, served, and passed an echo. The relay was stopped, and Redis (AOF on, `appendfsync everysec`) was restarted with `docker restart`. The namespace kept 23 of 23 keys, and Redis's `run_id` changed. `serve` then printed `tunnel-relay: Redis catalog connection failed; stage=authority_identity` and exited 1. `activate-first-incarnation` refused ("namespace already has a deployment incarnation; changing it requires recovery"), and `recovery-observe` refused ("recovery commands require a [recovery] configuration section"), which a one-relay configuration does not have and the guide does not document outside the cluster section. `recover` needs an external approval authority that is not shipped (M6-C22). A Redis restart with relays running closed every device session with reason `AUTHORITY_UNAVAILABLE`, and each `connect` exited 4. Section 2.3 said only a restart that loses the run (no persistence, or a restore) has this effect. That was wrong, because Redis draws a new run id at every start. **Docs corrected on `m6-dogfood-local`:** section 2.3 states it, and says the only way back in this alpha is a new `redis_namespace`. **Impact:** a host reboot, a Redis upgrade or a container restart ends the deployment. **Acceptance:** a single-relay operator can restart Redis with persistence and resume serving the same namespace, whether by a binding that survives a persisted restart or by a shipped, documented recovery path. Include a process-level test that restarts Redis between two `serve` runs. **Fly-specific evidence (from M6-C70's proof, formerly M6-C62):** measured with the deployment images (log nonce `m6c60-proof-20260923T093131Z-75524`, head `b459155`, 0 uncommitted paths, and two earlier runs): Redis restarted from its AOF volume with 24 of 24 keys and a new `run_id`, and a relay started afterwards exited 1 at `stage=authority_identity`. On Fly a Redis machine restarts on host maintenance, a crash, a `fly deploy` of the Redis app and any non-staged `fly secrets import` for it (so a Redis certificate rotation is one). A relay machine that starts after that exits 1 each time; its `[[restart]] policy = "on-failure", retries = 10` then leaves it `stopped`, `min_machines_running = 1` does not restart it, and `fly machine start` fails the same way until the namespace changes (from Fly's documented restart semantics and the measured exit, not observed on Fly). deploy-fly.md 6.4 and 6.5 give the new-namespace procedure. **Why the binding exists, re-derived from the code:** `activate-first-incarnation` writes `meta:redis_run_id`, and `SCRIPT_ENSURE_INCARNATION`, `LUA_DAY2_PRECONDITIONS`, and the owner claim, renew, release and current-owner scripts all require it to equal the run of the connection they execute on; each lane refused a reconnect to any other run. Within one Redis run the dataset has stayed in memory, so it cannot have lost or rolled back an acknowledged write; a new run can be an empty Redis, an older AOF/RDB or volume snapshot, a promoted replica, or a crash that lost `appendfsync everysec` writes, and a relay serving that could resurrect a revoked credential or grant or reuse an owner epoch. It is a continuity fence, and it fired on every restart because it cannot tell those from an in-place restart. **Design (scope: one Redis restarting in place from its own AOF; not a failover or restore path):** the fence stays; what satisfies it changes. The lanes of one catalog share a run binding (`crates/tunnel-catalog/src/redis/lane.rs`). Only a catalog that calls `enable_run_rebinding` -- `serve` without `[cluster]` -- may adopt another run; every other catalog, every `[cluster]` relay's included, refuses as before (the `m7-redis-lane-restart-verify.sh` gate is that witness). For an opted-in catalog, a lane reconnecting to a new run runs one atomic script (`SCRIPT_REBIND_RUN`) before any caller command: `unbound` for a namespace without incarnation or run binding, a refusal for another incarnation, adoption when the stored binding already names the new run (operator re-attestation or a sibling lane) **unless this process already refused that run for continuity**, and, with `redis_restart_continuity_seconds`, a token re-binding when all hold: `meta:continuity` equals a token this relay process wrote and Redis acknowledged (or one whose outcome it could not learn); that acknowledgement was at most one interval plus 5 s before the relay's last reply from the old run, so a token loop that stopped or kept failing while Redis answered does not count; and `CONFIG GET` on the new run shows `appendonly yes`, `appendfsync always`, `no-appendfsync-on-rewrite no` (else `class=persistence`; a refused `CONFIG GET` counts as unsound). `serve` checks the same three settings when it enables continuity and refuses to start otherwise, and the token loop reads them on the **bound** run after every token it writes: an acknowledgement counts for freshness only while they hold, so a runtime `CONFIG SET appendfsync everysec` (which a crash turns back into `always` from the configuration file, invisible to the new run's check) makes a later restart fail closed as `run_changed` once one interval plus 5 s has passed; a crash inside that bound can still lose about the last second of writes (operator.md says so, and not to change these settings at runtime). A supervisor turns token re-binding off and logs if the token loop ever ends. Scripts take the run id from the lane's verified connection at execution time, through a per-process random placeholder that no caller argument may resemble. A relay **started** after a restart has no token and is refused as `stage=authority_identity class=run_changed`; `tunnel-relay rebind-redis-run --config PATH --redis-restarted-in-place` re-binds it after the same `unbound`/incarnation checks and says the declaration was not verified. **What the token proves, and what it does not:** AOF replay restores a prefix of the command history, so a Redis holding the relay's last acknowledged token holds every write acknowledged before it, and with the three settings nothing acknowledged after it is lost by a restart or crash of that one Redis. It detects only a copy **older than the last token** (empty, or a snapshot, backup or replica taken before it). It is **not** sound across failover: a promoted asynchronous replica usually holds the last token and can lack writes the old primary acknowledged after it. A restore or replica taken within about one interval before Redis went away (plus any time the token loop was failing) also holds the token and can lack writes acknowledged after it, operator-CLI revocations included. `rebind-redis-run` cannot tell a restore or a promoted replica from an in-place restart at all: the flag is the operator's declaration. operator.md section 4 and deploy-fly.md 6.4 say so. Options rejected: a checksum or epoch stored only in Redis (a restored snapshot carries its own consistent copy); making `recover` usable without the external signer (M6-C22) for one relay (the same declaration with more machinery). New classes `unbound`, `run_changed`, `continuity`, `persistence` (M6-C72 vocabulary). The Fly Redis entrypoint now sets `no-appendfsync-on-rewrite no` explicitly (Redis's default; the live Fly Redis gets the line at its next rebuild, not changed here); the Fly `relay.toml` sets 5 s; the Fly relay entrypoint accepts `rebind-redis-run` (checked with `sh -n` only). **Evidence, real Redis:** `scripts/m6-redis-restart-verify.sh` (now also in CI's `m1-acceptance` job, which already runs the Docker-owning M1 restart gate; CI is billing-blocked, so it has not run there) runs `m6c65_redis_restart_keeps_the_namespace_and_refuses_lost_data` against its own `redis:8.4.0-alpine@sha256:6cbef353...` container (AOF, `appendfsync always`, `aof-load-truncated no`) on a free port; the shared 63790 Redis (which runs `appendfsync everysec`) is never restarted or reconfigured. | M6-C82 | [ ] A single relay started after a Redis restart cannot resume its namespace unattended: it has no continuity witness, so it refuses until an operator runs `rebind-redis-run`. | discovered defect (decision needed: options and a recommendation recorded) | unassigned (split from M6-C65 by the m6-c65-redis-restart worker) | From M6-C65's design: the continuity token a serving relay compares lives only in that process's memory, so a relay machine that restarts while Redis restarts (Fly host maintenance can move both), crashes, or is redeployed across a Redis restart exits 1 with `stage=authority_identity class=run_changed` and, on Fly, ends `stopped` after 10 restarts until someone runs deploy-fly.md 6.4's one-off `rebind-redis-run`. Accepting the namespace without a witness would accept a restored older snapshot too. **Acceptance:** a witness that survives the relay process and cannot be restored with Redis (for example the last acknowledged token persisted on a relay-owned volume, written before the relay treats it as acknowledged), a process-level test that restarts relay and Redis together and resumes, and the rollback and empty-Redis refusals of M6-C65's gate still red when defeated.<br><br>**m6-ops (2026-09-25): options and a recommendation, decision still needed.** Re-read at `f9f7abf`: the witness (`RunBinding`'s candidate set in `crates/tunnel-catalog/src/redis/lane.rs`) lives only in the serving process, and `serve` binds it at startup from nothing, so a relay that (re)starts after the Redis restart has no token to compare and M6-C65 correctly refuses. **(a) Persist the witness on a relay-owned volume** (the row's proposal): before `advance_restart_continuity` dispatches a token, append it as a candidate to a local file and `fsync` it; on an acknowledged write, rewrite the file to that single token and `fsync` before `continuity_acknowledged`; at startup, a namespace refused `run_changed` is re-bound when Redis holds a token the file holds, under the same persistence and freshness rules as a live relay (the freshness bound must then be measured against the file's acknowledgement time). Rollback protection holds because a restored older Redis cannot hold the newest acknowledged token; it fails if the file itself is restored from the same backup, so the file must live on storage that is never restored together with Redis, which operator.md would have to say. A missing or unreadable file is a refusal, not a pass. Costs: a writable persistent volume for every single relay (deploy-fly.md's relay has none today; a Fly volume is per machine, so a replaced machine falls back to refusal, which is safe), and one `fsync` per continuity interval. **(b) Let the deployment run `rebind-redis-run` automatically** (a Fly release command or a unit's `ExecStartPre`). Cheap, but it attests blindly: it accepts a Redis restored from an older snapshot, which is exactly what the fence exists to refuse. **(c) Accept and keep the manual step** documented in deploy-fly.md 6.4 and operator.md 4. **Recommendation: (a)**, with the process-level test the row asks for (restart relay and Redis together, resume unattended) and the existing M6-C65 rollback and empty-Redis refusals re-run red when defeated; never (b). **Owner decision needed:** whether a persistent relay volume is an acceptable requirement for single-relay deployments, and on Fly specifically. | — |

Suspected cause, not fully explained (see M6-C87): the M6-C79 held freeze could stall the connector-to-relay control path for up to about 2 s of ordinary traffic, and a stalled control path can lapse the stream's authorization. A true 2 s stall measured in isolation loses nothing, so the hosted losses under this hold are not accounted for by the stall length alone. | verified (hosted CI) | test harness (ci-linux-fixes worker; seen on hosted CI after #109) | **Observed.** Main `75adf25` run 35906580050, M2 default: `M2 continuous record 17524 written in relay phase active stage failed: harness timeout: M2 echo record response timed out`, relay `last_emitted=17553 peer_acked=17553 recv_contiguous=17552 terminal=true`, connector `emitted_sequences=17552,received_sequences=17553`. Probe run 35908765894, M2 accelerated: the same shape at record 110 (138 emitted against 139 received). **Mechanism, reproduced deterministically** in a Linux container. With the rotation interval raised to 60 s so no rotation interferes, the harness paused only the control connection's connector-to-relay direction at record 300 and kept round-tripping. A 1 s stall lost nothing. The stalls that lost an echo every time, with the hosted signature (emitted = received - 1) and the counters reading `unconfirmed_streams: 1, refreshes_in_flight: 1`, were nominally 2 s and 3 s. *Corrected in M6-C87:* those stalls in fact lasted until a round trip completed, at least 5 s. A true 2 s or 3 s stall loses nothing. The connector buffers a stream's input while its authorization refresh is unconfirmed, sends that refresh on the control path once the confirmed window has 1.5 s left, and on a lapse discards the buffered record. That record is input the connector has already transport-acknowledged to the relay (`peer_acked` reached it, so it is no longer in the relay's replay buffer) but never delivered. The hold's arming timed the next rotation from `active_since`, which was reset only on a *sampled* non-active phase. A rotation that completed between two samples left it stale, so the hold armed at once and paused for up to about 2 s with no rotation coming. That stall is the suspected trigger, not a measured cause. **Fix (harness):** `HoldArming` restarts the clock on every generation change. The hold now only *watches* (1 ms polls, no pause) until it sees `preparing`, and pauses only then, for at most 300 ms (`HELD_FREEZE_PAUSE_BUDGET`), well inside the refresh margin. **Tests:** `a_rotation_completed_between_samples_restarts_the_arming_clock` fails with the old reset rule (red, confirmed) and passes with the new one. `the_arming_rule_fires_on_preparing_and_once_per_generation` also passes. In the container, 8 of 8 accelerated runs held on the first try. **Diagnostics added:** the relay stream's authorization state, the relay's stream terminal events, and the connector's `StreamAuthCounters` now appear in the M2 failure snapshot. **The product defects this exposed are separate rows (M6-C86 and later):** a control stall that lapses authorization discards input the connector has transport-acknowledged, and the consumer is not told. **Review follow-ups (Opus, `b0ef9a3`):** a slow candidate attach can no longer turn the held freeze into a hard failure. The record is written only with at least 150 ms of the pause budget left (`HELD_FREEZE_WITNESS_RESERVE`). A record written but not witnessed in budget is round-tripped as an ordinary record, and that rotation is skipped. A frozen phase seen before `preparing` can still be held. `expired_streams` now counts streams, not calls.<br><br>**Verified on hosted CI (m6-verify, 2026-09-25).** Every completed M2 job on `main` whose head contains `fef7aa4` passed: 22 of 22 (runs 35923188596 to 36101353248; the 6 cancelled M2 jobs are not counted), each running the accelerated and the 300-second plans, e.g. CI run 36059280169 on `main` `5c2d907` (every job green), job 107833975670, `records_during_held_freeze=1` in both plans. That covers the harness fix; the unexplained part of the loss stays with M6-C87. | 2026-09-25T17:40:44+10:00 |

| M6-C87 | [ ] A control-path stall long enough to lapse a stream's authorization discards input the connector has already transport-acknowledged to the relay. After M6-C86 that is a prompt, typed failure, not a silent loss, but the stream still ends. | open (decision needed: options and a recommendation recorded) | connector and relay (found by the ci-linux-fixes worker through M6-C84) | **Measured tolerance, not a fix.** The relay's default `challenge_interval` is 2 s, so each confirmation grants about 2 s (`remaining_ms=1998` in a trace). The connector refreshes once 1.5 s is left, so every live stream refreshes about every 0.5 s. A refresh stuck behind a stalled control path leaves the stream unconfirmed, and its input buffered, until the confirmation arrives or the refresh's own 5 s deadline passes. In a Linux container with M6-C86 and M6-C88 applied, one record was sent 100 ms into a control-path stall of exactly N seconds: 2 s delivered 3 of 3, 3 s 3 of 3, 4 s 2 of 3, and 5.5 s 2 of 3. Every failure was a prompt consumer close as the stall ended, not a hang. Raising `M2_AUTH_REFRESH_MARGIN` to 3.5 s did not change the outcome, so the margin is not the bound. **Earlier numbers corrected:** the M6-C84 row's "a 2 s stall lost an echo" came from an experiment whose stall lasted until a round trip completed, which in practice meant at least 5 s. A true 2 s stall lost nothing. **Still open:** tolerating stalls beyond about 3 s would mean changing the relay's 2 s confirmation window or the connector's buffering rule, within the documented revocation bound (M6-C31). The hosted M6-C84 losses, under a hold of about 2 s at most, are not fully explained by these numbers.<br><br>**m6-ops (2026-09-25): options and a recommendation, decision still needed; not measured further here.** What the row measured bounds the tolerance at about 3 s and rules out the refresh margin (3.5 s changed nothing); it does not say which side discards the input once authorization lapses -- the relay's ~2 s confirmation window or the connector's 5 s refresh deadline -- so no option below should be chosen on reasoning alone. **(a) Lengthen the relay's confirmation window** (`challenge_interval`, 2 s default). Tolerance grows roughly with it, but so does the revocation bound operator.md documents for M6-C31 ("a stream already admitted ends within its 5 s authorization snapshot"), which is a security-visible promise. **(b) Change the connector's buffering rule**: hold unconfirmed input for a bounded window longer than one refresh deadline (bounded bytes per stream and per session) and dispatch it only once a confirmation arrives. Input that is held is not dispatched, so this does not weaken revocation; its costs are memory (already bounded by the stream credit window) and a later, still typed, failure when the stall outlasts the window. **(c) Take the refresh off the stalled path**: give authorization refreshes their own priority slot on the control socket so a stall in ordinary control traffic cannot delay them. Fixes local queueing stalls; does nothing for a network stall, which (b) covers. **Recommendation: first measure which side ends the stream** (one run with the relay's window raised to 4 s and one with the connector's refresh deadline raised to 10 s, the same N-second stall sweep as the row); then (b), plus (c) if the measurement shows local queueing, and not (a) unless the owner is willing to restate the revocation bound. **Owner decision needed** on (a)'s revocation trade if the measurement points at the relay window. | — |

AddrInUse`), and the reviewer saw `serve_rejects_corrupt_membership_state_through_the_binary` fail the same way in 1 of 5 runs. `free_tcp_addr`/`free_udp_addr` in `crates/tunnel-relay/tests/m7_startup.rs` bind port 0 and release it, and `assert_bindings_available` later re-binds the same port to prove the refused `serve` left nothing listening; on a host where other tests or processes open connections, the ephemeral port can be taken in between. Not a trivial fix, because the property under test is that `serve` bound nothing. **Acceptance:** a check that cannot be raced -- for example have the test hold its own listeners with `SO_REUSEPORT` off and assert `serve` fails to bind, or read the process's open sockets -- and 20 consecutive green runs under the workspace test load.<br><br>**ops-followups (2026-09-26): the fixture holds its addresses and releases only what `serve` binds (`0b852c0`).** `StartupFixture` now binds its consumer and device TCP listeners and its peer UDP socket and **holds** them (`held_consumer`, `held_device`, `held_peer`) instead of releasing them. **Finding while fixing it:** holding all three made 5 of the 13 cases fail every time with `tunnel-relay: Address already in use (os error 48)` -- `serve_rejects_corrupt_membership_state_through_the_binary`, `..._insecure_membership_state_...`, `..._unavailable_checkpoint_before_public_serving`, `serve_reaches_the_membership_check_when_redis_lanes_open_slowly` and `serve_sigterm_during_the_membership_bootstrap_exits_interrupted` (log `m7-startup-loop.log`, 20 of 20 runs). `serve` binds its consumer and device listeners (`crates/tunnel-relay/src/main.rs`, before the membership load) and, for the last two, the peer endpoint before those refusals, so the row's premise that "the property under test is that `serve` bound nothing" holds for the other 8 cases only; for these 5 the old re-bind proved only that the reaped process held nothing. **Now:** the 8 cases whose refusal precedes every bind keep all three addresses held, and `assert_bindings_available` proves the hold still refuses the relay's own bind calls (tokio's `TcpListener::bind`, with `SO_REUSEADDR`, and a plain UDP bind as quinn uses), so `serve` provably bound none of them; the 5 binding cases call `let_serve_bind_listeners` (consumer and device on port 0, which no other process can have taken) and the 2 that bind the peer call `let_serve_bind_peer` just before spawning. The peer port must be nonzero, so it is held from outside every common ephemeral range (20000-31999; Linux 32768-60999, macOS 49152-65535) and no automatic port assignment can take it in the moment before `serve` binds it. A released address is not re-bound after exit: the process has been reaped, the relay starts no child, and the kernel has closed its sockets; re-binding only raced other processes. `assert_failure` also refuses `already in use` in the diagnostics. **Could go red:** with the hold dropped and re-bound elsewhere, `serve_rejects_malformed_and_unknown_toml_before_any_listener` failed `the fixture must hold its address against the relay's TCP bind` (log `m6-c93-red.log`). **Residual, unchanged:** the two "closed port" helpers (`free_tcp_addr` for an unreachable Redis and checkpoint) still bind and release; another process *listening* there in the window would change the failure, not an `AddrInUse`. A bound-but-not-listening socket was tried and hung the Redis case on macOS, so it was reverted. **Evidence:** `cargo test --locked -p tunnel-relay --test m7_startup` 20 consecutive runs, 20 of 20 `test result: ok. 13 passed`, 0 `FAILED`, at `0b852c0` with 0 uncommitted paths, load average 91-110 from parallel agents (log nonce `opsfu-m7startup2-20260925T141249Z-94204`); workspace `cargo test --workspace --locked --no-fail-fast -- --test-threads=4` at `0e592686` exit 0, 155 of 155 `test result:` lines `ok`, 2,376 passed, 0 failed, 90 ignored (log nonce `opsfu-wstest1-20260925T152842Z-40172`); `cargo fmt --all -- --check` and `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets --locked -- -D warnings` exit 0 at `0e592686`.<br><br>**Review of PR #176 (2026-09-26, `3b3739e2`).** `serve_rejects_unavailable_checkpoint_before_public_serving` and `serve_sigterm_during_the_membership_bootstrap_exits_interrupted` release every address to `serve`, so their `assert_bindings_available` call checked nothing. It is removed from both, and `assert_bindings_available` now panics if no address is held. **Re-verified:** 10 of 10 `m7_startup` runs `13 passed` at `3b3739e2` through the limiter (log nonce `opsfu-m7startup-final2-20260925T230047Z-86600`). | 2026-09-26T09:04:55+10:00 |

Every earlier image deploy, onto a **running** relay, updated the machine in place and kept its ID (deploy-fly.md section 6.3). **Why it matters:** anything that records the relay's machine ID goes stale, including `fly machine restart <id>` and `fly logs --machine <id>` in the runbook. The documented expectation after a deploy (one started machine, both checks passing) is not met until someone starts it by hand, and nothing is served in the meantime. **Not known:** whether flyctl always replaces a stopped machine or did so here for another reason, and whether `fly secrets deploy` or `fly machine update` behaves differently.
